title: Issues in Australian Foreign Policy July to December 2023
abstract: From our first day in Government, we have worked to make Australia stronger in the world and safer at home. Investing in our capability and investing in our relationships, our deterrence and our diplomacy. And bringing both to our presence in this region. Engaging with our Pacific family with respect, reinvesting in development assistance, working with our neighbours and partners to promote peace, security, stability and prosperity right across the Indo-Pacific. Acknowledging the centrality of ASEAN to our north. And supporting Ukraine in the face of the illegal and immoral invasion by Russia. We know there is no security in isolation … A partnership with two of Australia's oldest friends, through AUKUS, and an enhancement of the alliance that is the heart of one of the three pillars of our foreign policy. Is consistent with the Labor values that I have been a part of my whole life. Our US alliance. Regional engagement. Support for multilateralism … We have to analyse the world as it is rather than how we would want it to be.1 Australia continued to commit to US strategy in the Indo-Pacific and the rest of the world. While foreign policy has clearly shifted under the Albanese government, it appears that Australia has no real appetite for developing “a middle path for a middle power”.2 Australia has long been trying to ‘balance’ its major security and economic partners, whilst knowing full well that security relationships ultimately matter most. Harking back to the China choice debate, it's now clearer than ever that Australia will ‘choose’ the United States if conflict were to occur between the United States and China, if it were ever in doubt! Still, Australia does not want to make an exclusive choice unless it must. Clearly, good relations with China are beneficial for the Australian economy and the period under review saw marked improvements in the relationship, which was a win for those exporters previously shut out of the Chinese market. The Hamas attack on Israel and the subsequent Israeli military response was the dominant international news story of the six-month period. The Israel/Palestine issue fits uncomfortably into the US-centric Australian security framework, with the government concerned not to differ too much from the US position of unequivocal support for Israel. This is despite Albanese's previous support for the Palestinian cause and his status as a founding member of the Parliamentary Friends of Palestine group.3 While the United States eventually made some efforts to temper the intensity of the Israeli response and provide support for the people of Gaza, there were huge casualties - including many children – and the widescale destruction of buildings and infrastructure. In the final days of the year, the Israeli military response led South Africa to institute proceedings against Israel in the International Court of Justice. Israel/Palestine comes and goes as a significant issue for Australian foreign policy, inserting itself into the policy sphere in reaction to events on the ground in the Middle East. It is the possibility of a wider Middle Eastern conflict that will perhaps dominate coming periods of review. Another clear theme of the period was a continuation of the Albanese government's efforts to engage with the Indo-Pacific, with Ministers connected to the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade making regular visits and engaging with the Pacific Island Countries (PICs), Southeast Asia and India.4 Leaders committed to the transition away from coal, oil and gas in our energy systems, in line with IPCC pathways for limiting global average temperatures to 1.5°C above preindustrial levels with a peak in fossil fuel consumption in the near term.6 The objective of Australia's development program is to advance an Indo-Pacific that is peaceful, stable, and prosperous. A region that is predictable—where differences are resolved by international law and norms, and where we can cooperate, trade, and thrive. To achieve this requires sustainable development and lifting people out of poverty.9 Wong nominates the Pacific first among her accomplishments as foreign minister. She cites Australia's new security agreements with Papua New Guinea, Tuvalu and Vanuatu. And the newly created Pacific Engagement Visa, which she describes as “a change in the way in which we engage with the Pacific, playing much more to our strengths”. This new category grants permanent residency to 3000 Pacific islanders a year initially, offering them a future in Australia rather than transient working rights.11 Wong attended the Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) Foreign Ministers' Meeting in Suva in mid-September, meeting with Fijian Prime Minister and Minister for Foreign Affairs Sitiveni Rabuka to “discuss enhancing our Partnership, strengthening our economies, responding to the climate crisis and delivering for our shared regional interests”.15 The following month Wong announced the new Pacific Engagement Visa, which “will enable up to 3,000 nationals of Pacific Island countries and Timor-Leste to migrate to Australia as permanent residents each year [and] create new opportunities for the people of the Pacific and Timor-Leste to live, work and be educated in Australia – strengthening diaspora communities, and encouraging greater cultural, business and educational exchange”.16 This was followed up in November with additional support for Pacific Engagement Visa holders and Pacific Australia Labour Mobility scheme families including access to Medicare, student loans, family tax benefits and the child care subsidy.17 In mid-October the Prime Minister of Fiji Sitiveni Rabuka embarked on a 4-day official Guest of Government visit. At Bilateral talks during the visit, Albanese and Rabuka – in a Joint Statement – noted that the “updated Vuvale Partnership elevates our shared commitment to tackling climate change and strengthening our economic and trade partnership. It also has an increased focus on human development, First Nations' peoples and culture, skills development and cyber security”.18 In early November, Albanese and Conroy attended the Pacific Islands Forum Leaders' Meeting in the Cook Islands. According to Albanese “Australia sees the Pacific as family and none of us can achieve the future we want alone”.19 Whilst at the Forum Albanese “briefed Leaders on the Government's action to reduce Australia's emissions and build our clean energy industries”.20 Commitments included $350 million for regional climate infrastructure, including $75 million for “off-grid and community scale renewable energy in remote and rural parts of the Pacific”. There would also be a contribution to the Pacific Resilience Facility and the Green Climate Fund. Albanese and the Prime Minister of Tuvalu Kausea Natano also announced the elevation of the bilateral relationship to “a more advanced, integrated and comprehensive partnership – the Falepili Union”.21 After the Forum Albanese talked up “Australia's commitment to deepening its engagement in the Pacific and addressing the shared challenges facing us all, including shaping a peaceful, stable and prosperous Pacific, and the impacts of climate change”.22 In early December the Prime Minister of Papua New Guinea, James Marape visited Australia for an official visit. Australia and PNG signed a Bilateral Security Agreement: “a legally-binding framework to deepen our security cooperation – in traditional areas of defence, policing, border and maritime security, and also non-traditional areas of cyber security, climate change, gender-based violence and critical infrastructure”.23 The Agreement “fulfils a commitment under our Comprehensive Strategic and Economic Partnership”. Albanese also announced a $200 million commitment to Papua New Guinea's “national security priorities”, which will provide “full circle support for Papua New Guinea's internal security, from police to courts to correctional services”. Continuing on the security theme, Defence Minister Richard Marles visited New Caledonia “to participate in the eighth annual South Pacific Defence Ministers' Meeting (SPDMM), hosted by France”. Whilst there he held bilateral meetings with SPDMM nations, including the host, France, “to discuss Australia and France's growing defence relationship”. During the six-month period, Australia provided a Guardian-class Patrol Boat and two new PAC 750 light transport aircraft to Papua New Guinea, and a Guardian-class Patrol Boat, the Nafanua III, to Samoa. Australia also signed a bilateral security agreement with Vanuatu in mid-December. Australian policy-makers also engaged with their New Zealand counterparts during the period. As usual at these events, the two Prime Ministers noted that the relationship “is unlike any other,” wherein “shared values, common outlook and people-to-people links underpin a critical partnership”. main_argument: Australia's foreign policy under the Albanese government prioritizes strengthening alliances, especially with the US via AUKUS, deepening regional engagement with Pacific and Southeast Asian partners, and advancing a stable, prosperous Indo-Pacific amid global geopolitical tensions.
research_design: Qualitative policy analysis examining government statements, bilateral agreements, and diplomatic engagements from July to December 2023.
method: Descriptive and interpretive analysis of official speeches, government announcements, bilateral visits, and multilateral meetings.
dataset_or_evidence: Public records of Australian government foreign policy statements, security agreements, visa policy announcements, and bilateral/multilateral diplomatic activities during the period.
unit_of_analysis: Australian foreign policy actions and diplomatic relations with key partners (US, Pacific Island countries, Southeast Asia, New Zealand) during the specified period.
time_period_studied: July to December 2023
geographic_focus: Indo-Pacific region, including Pacific Island countries, Southeast Asia, Australia, New Zealand, and engagement with US and Middle East contexts.
identification_strategy: Chronological tracing of policy shifts and diplomatic initiatives reflecting Australia's strategic priorities and responses to regional and global developments.
key_findings: The Albanese government has reinforced the US alliance via AUKUS, expanded security partnerships with Pacific nations, introduced Pacific Engagement Visa to strengthen people-to-people ties, committed substantial resources to climate and security issues in the region, and maintained a pragmatic balance with China while unequivocally supporting US positions in key conflicts. Engagement with New Zealand remains close, emphasizing shared values and economic ties.
main_limitations: Analysis relies on publicly available texts and official statements, which may underrepresent internal policy debates or dissenting views; limited quantitative data restricts assessment of long-term impact.
ir_scholars_relevance: Provides valuable insight into middle-power diplomacy amid great power competition, regional security dynamics, alliance politics, and the integration of climate and security policy in the Indo-Pacific.
strategic_infrastructure_relevance: Highlights Australia's efforts to secure critical infrastructure and capacity in the Indo-Pacific through security agreements addressing maritime, cyber, and climate-related vulnerabilities, alongside investments in renewable energy infrastructure in the Pacific, illustrating the intersection of strategic infrastructure and foreign policy.

Time period studied: July to December 2023

Geographic focus: Indo-Pacific region, including Pacific Island countries, Southeast Asia, Australia, New Zealand, and engagement with US and Middle East contexts.

Identification strategy: Chronological tracing of policy shifts and diplomatic initiatives reflecting Australia's strategic priorities and responses to regional and global developments.

Engagement with New Zealand remains close, emphasizing shared values and economic ties.

Main limitations: Analysis relies on publicly available texts and official statements, which may underrepresent internal policy debates or dissenting views; limited quantitative data restricts assessment of long-term impact.

title: Review of “Examining US-China-Russia Foreign Relations: Great Power Politics in a Post-Obama Era”
abstract: In Examining US-China-Russia Foreign Relations: Great Power Politics in a Post-Obama Era, G.O. Hall investigates how the three powers coordinate, engage, contain and confront one another in shaping the world order after Obama’s presidency. President Obama had proposed a Tripolar Conflict, Cooperation and Competition (TC3) model. Dr Gregory O. Hall further analyzes how the relevance of American double axes (US–China, Axis-1; US–Russia, Axis-2) has evolved in grappling with the global issues and the regional crises.From my point of view, Hall engages in international relations (IR) and diplomatic studies and provides a comprehensive delineation of the contemporary strategic triangle. Each is scrambling for its respective political, economic, military and cultural advantage, dominance and discourse power by handling a series of international and regional incidents. Rather than exploring arcane IR theories such as realism, neorealism, neoclassical realism and constructivism, Hall focuses on the transformative trajectories of US foreign policies towards China and Russia during Trump’s and Biden’s administrations by drawing on many domestic and international cases.This book is divided into three parts. The first part of the book, composed of three chapters, describes how the relatively smooth and palliative relations within the two US axes of the triangle since the end of the Cold War were progressively worsening. Each was mostly accountable to the individual leaders, their attributes and the domestic variables (p. 3, Chapter 1) when faced with a range of multifarious and complicated situations and environments. USSR was dismantled in late 1991, and Russia declined thereafter. Meanwhile, China gained strength as an ascendant global power in the early 2000s. It gradually assembled a group of states such as Brazil, India, Saudi Arabia and South Africa of the Global South to challenge America’s post-war unipolar hegemony as influential regional or emerging global powers in a multilateral arena. This mirrors the current intricate background of US–China–Russia strategic triangle of competition, antagonism and confrontation. According to Hall, China and the Global South are reshaping the contours of the Liberal International Order. The power shift among the great powers generally favors China and the non-Western world overall (p. 4, Chapter 1), which adequately demonstrates the shift of the global balance of power to the global south and east.China’s low profile in accomplishing its rapid rise has posed a major threat to US foreign policy and strategic considerations in recent years. Especially with Xi Jinping’s coming to power in 2013 and subsequent China’s overt wolf warrior diplomacy, a confrontational form of public diplomacy adopted by diplomats of the People’s Republic of China in the late 2010s, the Washington-Beijing dyad has become the more predominant axis within the tripolar conflict. Consequently discords have repeatedly emerged between both sides concerning cybersecurity, human rights, the Taiwan issue, trade dispute and technology theft. Therefore, China has apparently become the shaper of the new post-war international order, replacing Russia. According to Thomas Wright, the senior director for strategic planning at the USA National Security Council, with neo-authoritarianism on the rise, the old assumptions undergirding a common set of Western values just will not do (Wright, 2018, p. 1). In addition, with the advent of globalization and the increasingly decisive role of intergovernmental and transnational organizations in the 21st century, conflicts among the major powers began to occur on numerous international occasions.Apart from the foreign policy executives and the different type of political systems, realistic factors such as the domestic environment and external dynamics have constituted the most critical analytical factors for understanding the US–China–Russia relationships. Examples include America’s abrupt policy shift from domestic issues to global anti-terrorism since 9/11, 2001, Russia’s hedge and support for Syria and Iran and China’s significant increase in its voice and influence in the international system. These led to the belief that Robert Keohane and Joseph Nye’s “interdependence theory” is obsolete and inapplicable to the new realities. In their opinions, the interdependency theory in international relations represents a buffer between the concepts of dependence and independence in relations between and among nation states in the international milieu. On the basis of his constant observations, Hall argues that nowadays the tripolar’s relationship is more like a combative pattern than an interdependent mode. In Hall’s opinion, many observers would agree that the international system is in a state of transition at this time, gravitating towards a multipolar order. China has risen to global prominence on the various measures of hard and soft power. National actors like Iran, Saudi Arabia and Turkey are regional powers. The current state may become either some form of US–Chinese bipolarity or a “messy” multipolar/multilevel/multilateral order (p. 13, Chapter 1). However, China is selective in its use of force as a bid to promote/maintain multipolarity, and hence prevent others’ infringement of its position (Wang and Song, 2016, p. 60). I do not fully agree with the multipolarity view, because no other country has emerged yet to challenge the predominant position of the Big Three (the USA, China and Russia), even though the EU, Japan, India and the UK are not negligible powers.The strategic triangulation of the US–China–Russia interrelationships began in the 1960s and 1970s against the background of the Cold War, when the mutually hostile and militarily confrontational model prevailed. Thanks to several subsequent prominent leaders’ deliberations and foresight, among them Richard M. Nixon, Jimmy E. Carter, Mao Zedong, Ronald W. Reagan, Mikhail S. Gorbachev and Boris N. Yeltsin, great power relations incrementally returned to détente and moderation in the 1990s and at the turn of the new century. In Hall’s view, the resilient strategic triangle dynamic is playing an important role in ushering in a multipolar order; however, Beijing and Moscow use their own bilateral relationship and their ties with other players to counter Washington’s influence (p. 20–21, Chapter 2). As for China, multi-lateral initiatives and regional associations such as the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO), Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), BRICS (Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa), the New Development Bank (NDB), the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) have become a frontline vis-à-vis US-led alliances. These include the USA, UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand (the Five Eyes), the Australia, UK, the USA (AUKUS), the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue (Quad) between Australia, India, Japan and the USA, which reinforce the US power and help it consolidate and promote its Indo-Pacific Strategy. The two powers ─ the USA and China ─ are thus endeavoring to win over partners and engage in all-around competition.Though China is playing a limited role in shaping global norms and rules and its reputed role as a “price taker [1],” Loh, 2024, p. 4). However, according to the American government’s assessment, the most comprehensive and serious challenge to US national security is the PRC’s coercive and increasingly aggressive endeavor to refashion the Indo-Pacific region and the international system to suit its interests and authoritarian preferences (O’Rourke, 2024, p. 4). As a result, the adverse situation arising from taking an aggressive stance is that China’s trade and investment opportunities were at risk, because China’s leaders only wanted the benefits of a modern economy, but were not willing to create a more open society (Haass, 2017, p. 88).China is becoming the main challenger as a global power in the economic and military spheres, and Russia sees itself as a great power in military strength and natural resources. As a result, the USA may be inadequate in leading the free world versus the neo-authoritarian world, because the former have practically bonded with many regional national actors to grow their international prominence. For that matter, in Part II, Hall reconsiders agency and context in the foreign affairs of the great powers, especially the domestic stimuli in redirecting their diplomatic policies and external discourse. Over the years, China’s implementation of Marxist-Leninist thought, its dream of becoming a superpower, and Xi’s strong leadership, complete with Sino-Russian military cooperation and the Xi-Putin’s personal closeness have further fractured and intensified the triad’s resultant hostility and collisions. One reason is that none of the parties are willing to give in or acknowledge the other side’s political institutions and primacy. In addition, the trilateral sides have been engaging in tit-for-tat in negotiating and in resolving issues such as human rights, economic models, domestic conflicts, energy security, climate change and Russian invasion of Ukraine. Each of these, whether domestic or external, may trigger severe diplomatic and military disputes. From the perspective of the USA, the Sino-Russian partnership poses a “very serious problem”. Public sentiment within the two US axes of the strategic triangle complements and perhaps even reinforces views in the governmental sphere (p. 76, Chapter 6).In the concluding part, Hall makes an appeal to governments of all nations to collaborate to tackle numerous challenges and crises. He recommends this especially because he sees global powers continuing to trend towards the non-western world, and because the world of today looks a lot less like the world of the late 20th century (p. 128, Chapter 8). In his view, to avert conflicts and confrontations, the Big Three should exercise restraints and enhance dialogue and communication in handling the international issues. The dominant factor in the future is that domestic concerns appear to be rising to the fore in great power politics. They will probably become the major variables in transforming the relationship among the major powers. Of special note, nowadays, all countries have come to recognize that the future competition among countries will happen in the domains of high-tech, military, culture and values. The Russia–Ukraine War is central to all these domains, although, from Russia’s perspective, this unpopular aggression is nothing more than a dynamic squabble with once brotherly Ukraine (Kortunov, 2019, p. 27).In the introduction, Hall tells the reader that the book is primarily for students, scholars and practitioners of international relations, international affairs and foreign policy (p. xv, preface). I have found the book to be a professional monograph dedicated to analyzing the current evolution of the relationship between the USA, China and Russia, with detailed documents, numerous case studies and eclectic subjects. However, international relations are changing rapidly and are tough and unpredictable. Hall cannot make a reasonable prediction where the tripolar relationship will be redirected, but he again reflects on the key hot spots such as NATO’s eastward expansion, issues of Georgia and Ukraine, which will trigger an escalating international situation.This book seemed to me to be too conservative and hesitant in determining the role of the European Union and NATO in the Russia-Ukraine War. In addition, it does not employ visible cases to cast light on how the domestic environment of the USA affects the presidential election and the USA foreign relations with particular countries. In addition, Hall’s proposing structure still matters in international affairs, which obscures whether the international organizations or the rectangular political, military and economic structure among the three powers matter most in affecting the imminent trends and events. Furthermore, there is also a lack of in-depth discussion on how the Syrian issue and the Iranian issue impact the international situation, which can probably become the most potential Grey Rhino incidents to profoundly influence the international context.
main_argument: The US-China-Russia strategic triangle is evolving from post-Cold War détente to intensified competition shaped by domestic politics, leadership, and shifting global power dynamics, with China emerging as the predominant challenger in a transitioning multipolar order.
research_design: Qualitative, interpretive analysis integrating historical context, contemporary case studies, and foreign policy trajectories during Trump and Biden administrations.
method: Analytical narrative based on synthesis of secondary sources, official documents, and international incidents illustrating diplomatic, economic, and military interactions.
dataset_or_evidence: Domestic and international cases, foreign policy shifts, intergovernmental initiatives, and quotations from policymakers and scholars (e.g., Thomas Wright, O’Rourke).
unit_of_analysis: Great powers (United States, China, Russia) and their bilateral and trilateral relationships within the global strategic order.
time_period_studied: Post-Obama era (2013 onwards, focusing primarily on Trump and Biden administrations) with historical background from Cold War to present.
geographic_focus: Global, with emphasis on the Indo-Pacific region, Eurasia, and multilateral organizations involving these powers.
identification_strategy: Contextual and process tracing to relate domestic political factors and leadership profiles to shifts in bilateral/trilateral foreign policies and strategic postures.
key_findings: China has supplanted Russia as the main challenger to US dominance, leveraging multilateral initiatives to contest US-led alliances. Domestic politics and leadership styles critically influence the dynamics of the tripolar relationship, which is increasingly confrontational rather than interdependent. The US seeks to consolidate alliances (e.g., AUKUS, Quad) to offset China's rise, but multipolarity remains fluid and contested.
main_limitations: Lacks empirical testing or quantitative analysis; insufficient focus on EU and NATO roles; limited exploration of domestic political impacts on US elections and diplomacy; minimal analysis of Middle East issues affecting global order.
ir_scholars_relevance: Provides a comprehensive contemporary synthesis of great power competition that moves beyond traditional IR theories, emphasizing domestic drivers and multipolarity dynamics crucial for understanding evolving US-China-Russia relations.
strategic_infrastructure_relevance: Addresses strategic infrastructure indirectly through discussions of military and technological competition, multilateral initiatives like the Belt and Road, and alliances (AUKUS, Five Eyes), relevant for understanding geopolitical strategy and the technological-ideological rivalry shaping global governance.

Research design: Qualitative, interpretive analysis integrating historical context, contemporary case studies, and foreign policy trajectories during Trump and Biden administrations.

Method: Analytical narrative based on synthesis of secondary sources, official documents, and international incidents illustrating diplomatic, economic, and military interactions.

Dataset or evidence: Domestic and international cases, foreign policy shifts, intergovernmental initiatives, and quotations from policymakers and scholars (e.g., Thomas Wright, O’Rourke).

Unit of analysis: Great powers (United States, China, Russia) and their bilateral and trilateral relationships within the global strategic order.

Time period studied: Post-Obama era (2013 onwards, focusing primarily on Trump and Biden administrations) with historical background from Cold War to present.

Geographic focus: Global, with emphasis on the Indo-Pacific region, Eurasia, and multilateral organizations involving these powers.

Identification strategy: Contextual and process tracing to relate domestic political factors and leadership profiles to shifts in bilateral/trilateral foreign policies and strategic postures.

Key findings: China has supplanted Russia as the main challenger to US dominance, leveraging multilateral initiatives to contest US-led alliances. Domestic politics and leadership styles critically influence the dynamics of the tripolar relationship, which is increasingly confrontational rather than interdependent. The US seeks to consolidate alliances (e.g., AUKUS, Quad) to offset China's rise, but multipolarity remains fluid and contested.

Main limitations: Lacks empirical testing or quantitative analysis; insufficient focus on EU and NATO roles; limited exploration of domestic political impacts on US elections and diplomacy; minimal analysis of Middle East issues affecting global order.

Why this matters for IR scholars: Provides a comprehensive contemporary synthesis of great power competition that moves beyond traditional IR theories, emphasizing domestic drivers and multipolarity dynamics crucial for understanding evolving US-China-Russia relations.

Why this matters for strategic infrastructure research: Addresses strategic infrastructure indirectly through discussions of military and technological competition, multilateral initiatives like the Belt and Road, and alliances (AUKUS, Five Eyes), relevant for understanding geopolitical strategy and the technological-ideological rivalry shaping global governance.

title: Corridors, pipelines and electrons: modalities of economic engagement by central Asia with the Indo-Pacific
abstract: Abstract This article explores the evolving economic statecraft strategies of landlocked central Asian states towards the Indo-Pacific region. Employing an analytical framework termed ‘omni-enmeshment’, the article argues that the strategies of some central Asian countries transcend mere hedging tactics by actively fostering deep integration with key Indo-Pacific actors like China, South Korea, India, Japan, Iran and the United Arab Emirates. This theoretical framework is complemented by empirical evidence of engagement through infrastructural pathways such as trade and transport corridors, energy pipelines and renewable energy projects. The study is guided by two specific questions. First, how is economic statecraft operationalized by the central Asian states? Second, why have central Asian states become more effective, in some cases, at wielding the tools of economic statecraft in their relations with Indo-Pacific nations? Methodologically, the research is a qualitative, narrative review supported by a rich and diverse array of secondary data. The article contributes to broader discussions on the domestic and geopolitical aspects of intra- and extraregional economic integration, as well as the agency of smaller states and middle powers, highlighting central Asia's role in recalibrating its relations within the evolving Indo-Pacific landscape.

title: Access Denied? The Sino-American Contest for Military Primacy in Asia
abstract: Abstract How has the balance of power shifted in maritime East Asia, and what does this change mean for the U.S.-China military competition in the region? We examine these questions by focusing on a central pillar of U.S. military might—land-based air power—in the context of a war over Taiwan. We create a new, unclassified, and transparent model of a Taiwan conflict, which allows users to explore multiple scenarios, alternative U.S. basing options, various People's Liberation Army attack strategies, and a range of potential U.S. defensive enhancements to see how those alternatives influence outcomes. We find that: (1) the United States' current approach to defend Taiwan exposes U.S. forces to significant risk of catastrophic defeat; (2) the U.S. Air Force's answer to this problem is both unlikely to work and escalatory; and (3) a combination of hardening air bases and enhancing missile defenses and local jamming at U.S. facilities is a better option. More broadly, U.S. national security policy toward China approaches an inflection point. The United States can lean in and significantly enhance the resilience of its forces in East Asia; lean back and rely more on instruments of military power that are less vulnerable to China's regional defense systems; or reconsider its broader geopolitical goals in the region. The current path, seeking to deter Chinese attacks with a vulnerable forward-based military posture, courts disaster.
main_argument: The U.S. military’s current forward-based air power strategy in defending Taiwan is highly vulnerable to Chinese attack, risking catastrophic defeat; a strategy focusing on hardening bases and enhancing defensive countermeasures is more viable.
research_design: Scenario-based modeling of a potential war over Taiwan using a transparent, unclassified simulation to compare alternative U.S. basing and Chinese attack strategies.
method: Development and simulation of a detailed military conflict model incorporating various U.S. and PLA strategies and defensive enhancements.

identification_strategy: Comparative scenario simulation varying basing options, attack profiles, and defense enhancements to identify conditions most likely to yield favorable outcomes.
key_findings: Current U.S. forward-based air power posture is highly vulnerable; proposed Air Force responses risk escalation and are unlikely effective; combined base hardening, missile defenses, and electronic countermeasures offer a more resilient defense option; U.S. policy faces a critical choice between enhancing resilience, relying less on vulnerable postures, or reconsidering broader strategic goals.
main_limitations: Model assumptions may oversimplify complex operational realities; excludes classified intelligence and dynamic political variables; limited to military-technical simulations without factoring in political or strategic decision-making nuances.
ir_scholars_relevance: Provides empirical modeling insights into great power military competition in Asia, illustrating how military posture influences balance of power and regional stability; informs debates on deterrence, escalation risks, and alliance strategy.
strategic_infrastructure_relevance: Highlights the vulnerability and strategic importance of U.S. military infrastructure in Asia, underlining the need for resilient basing and defensive technologies to maintain power projection amid China's growing regional capabilities.

title: The positive externalities of US–China institutional balancing in the Indo-Pacific
abstract: Abstract Challenging the pessimistic and alarmist view of competition between the United States and China, we propose a soft balancing argument—institutional balancing for peace (shortened to ‘institutional peace’)—to highlight the positive outcomes of their strategic rivalry. We argue that globalization, economic interdependence and nuclear deterrence have motivated the US and China to engage in institutional balancing to vie for security, power and influence in the international system. We examine how the US and China have used multilateral and minilateral security institutions, such as various trilateral dialogue mechanisms, the Quad, the Shangri-La Dialogue, the Conference on Interaction and Confidence-building Measures in Asia and the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, to compete in the Indo-Pacific region in the period since the 2008 global financial crisis. We suggest that institutional balancing between the US and China has led to three positive externalities for the region: sustained institutional dynamism, new incentives for regional cooperation and the provision of public goods, unintentionally fostering regional peace and prosperity in the long run. If the United States and China can manage their strategic competition through international institutions, the emerging transition of the international order may be more peaceful than historical transitions, even amid potential regional military crises.
main_argument: US-China institutional balancing in the Indo-Pacific generates positive externalities by fostering peace, cooperation, and regional prosperity despite strategic rivalry.
research_design: Qualitative case study analysis of institutional balancing through multilateral and minilateral security organizations post-2008.
method: Descriptive and interpretive analysis of institutional behaviors and outcomes within selected Indo-Pacific security forums.
dataset_or_evidence: Security institutions such as the Quad, Shangri-La Dialogue, CICA, and Shanghai Cooperation Organisation since the 2008 global financial crisis.
unit_of_analysis: US-China interactions within Indo-Pacific multilateral and minilateral security institutions.
time_period_studied: 2008 to present (post-global financial crisis period).
geographic_focus: Indo-Pacific region.
identification_strategy: Comparative institutional observation highlighting outputs and externalities of US-China balancing within security forums.
key_findings: Institutional balancing has led to sustained institutional dynamism, enhanced incentives for regional cooperation, and the provision of public goods, which collectively support regional peace and prosperity.
main_limitations: Lacks quantitative validation; potential overemphasis on positive externalities without systematically addressing instances where rivalry undermines institutions.
ir_scholars_relevance: Challenges alarmist views of great power rivalry by offering a nuanced perspective on institutional balancing as a mechanism mitigating conflict and fostering order during systemic transitions.
strategic_infrastructure_relevance: Relevant for understanding how strategic competition over regional security infrastructure and governance can produce stabilizing institutional outcomes in the Indo-Pacific.

title: Geopolitics of the Indo-Pacific: Strategic Competition, Alliances, and Regional Security
abstract: The Indo-Pacific has become the epicenter of the twenty-first century geopolitical conflict, the main arena of strategic competition, development of alliances, and regional security. The paper discusses how Indo-Pacific geopolitics is multidimensional, taking a closer look at the U.S.China rivalry, emergence of flexible minilateral security arrangements, and how different countries in the regions respond to this. The study relies on a qualitative research design entailing a thematic content analysis of academic literature, policy reports, and think tank publications, and finds three key dynamics to be resourcing the regional security architecture: first, the escalation of the great-power competition promoted by the aggressive maritime expansion of China and by the forward-deployed deterrence of the United States; second, the transformation of the alliances that go beyond rigid bilateralism to fluid minilateral constructs like Quad and AUKUS that would increase the regional interoperability without establishing formal treaty relations; third, the hedging strategies The finding also points out how the aspect of non-traditional security menace, such as cyberattacks, grey-zone activities, unlawful fishing, and climate-based susceptibility, is rising to prominence and becoming a burden as far as conventional security protocols are concerned. The work should be added to the literature on international security and Indo-Pacific strategy as an amalgam of historical military competition and economic statecraft and hybrid threat, whereby a flexible, multilayered and inclusive regional security architecture was required, which could help the balancing of deterrence and cooperation.

INTRODUCTION  
This large swath stretching across the eastern coast of Africa to the Indian Ocean and further out to the western 
Pacific Ocean, came to be recognized as the stage where great power competition internationally will o ccur, 
especially between the United States and China, in the 21 st century. The significance of the region is also enabled 
by its economic dynamism as it contributes more than 60 percent of world GDP and harbors the most critical 
maritime chokepoints, including the South China Sea and straight of Malacca (International Institute for Strategic 
Studies [IISS], 2024). In its modern usage, Indo-Pacific refers to a strategic coding of the Indian and Pacific features 
as an interconnected sea area and has been viewed as a modification of geopolitical statements used by nations such 
as Japan, Australia, India, and the United States since about 2010 (Wilkins, 2025). 
In the last ten years, strategic rivalry in the area has been heightening with China currently having an aggressive 
maritime policy as it continues to extend its influence in the South China Sea, acquisitions of ports in the Indian 
Ocean as well as growing technology advancements when it comes to missiles and naval forces. The United States 
has responded to this by increasing the number of freedom of navigation operations, forward military presence, and

strengthened regional alliances (Raska, 2019; Indo -Pacific Studies Center [IPSC], 2025). Such a dynamic has 
excited the shift toward regional security architecture in the region, a shift away from the bilateral alliance system to 
the emergence of minilateral systems like the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue (Quad) and AUKUS (Wilkins, 2025; 
“San Francisco System,” 2025). 
The Quad, which is a group comprising th e United States, Japan, India, and Australia, has taken a new form 
developed through the foundation of the informal discussion to an important strategic dialogue over maritime 
security, supply chain resilience and infrastructure development (Quadrilateral Security Dialogue, 2025). AUKUS, 
established in 2021, institutionalised trilateral security collaboration amid Australia, the United Kingdom, and the 
United States to focus on nuclear -powered submarines, the cyberspace, and artificial intelligence (AUKUS, 2025). 
These groupings are indicators of a shift to the type of utilitarian, capability‑based coordination as opposed to formal 
treaty alliances. 
Nevertheless, several Southeast Asian and mid-powers engage in strategic hedging, where they attempt to maintain a 
third path by avoiding alignment and economic deepening with unilateralism, regardless of communist 
distinctiveness (Vu Lam, 2025). According to the 2024 Intelligence Review, Australian Government has argued that 
a major-power conflict is no longer unimaginable, with coercion and disinformation, as well as cyber threats among 
the increasing challenges to the security of the region (Australian Government, 2025). The 2025 Shangri‑La 
Dialogue also raised issues of the region, as U. S. defense leaders stre ssed on the need to embark on increased 
deterrence and yet the regional powers handled security issues against the need of economic interdependence 
(Hegseth, 2025). 
This combination of strategic rivalry, changes of alliances, and security concerns of a reg ion is at the heart of this 
investigation. This raises important questions: How are strategic competition and the Indo -Pacific interacting with 
one another? What are the adaptations or emerging structures of alliances? What does this portend on regional 
security? This paper attempts to explicate the current and emerging geopolitical situation of the Indo -Pacific by 
juxtaposing strategic theory with practical alliance behavior. 
LITERATURE REVIEW 
Historical Evolution of the Indo-Pacific Concept 
The Indo -Pacific has in the recent past transformed to be a key strategic thinking position in geopolitics as an 
extension of geographical observation. There were already precedents in which Alfred Thayer Mahan already 
outlined the role of the Indian and P acific Oceans in global maritime supremacy and presagged the importance of 
the region to the 21 st century (Mahan, 1890/2013). During the post -Cold War, the Asia -Pacific became the main 
term of the regional rhetoric, stressing on alliances of the U.S. in E ast Asia and trans -Pacific economic patterns 
(Friedberg, 2012). But in the 2010s, policymakers and researchers have started to give priority to the Indo-Pacific to 
reflect growing strategic integration between the region of the Indian Ocean and the region of the Western Pacific 
(Medcalf, 2020). 
This was a shift in geopolitics, including the economic outreaches of India to the east, China to the west with its Belt 
and Road Initiative (BRI), and the calls by Australia and Japan to a free and open Indo -Pacific (Heiduk & Wacker, 
2020; Grare, 2021). Researchers underline the fact that the Indo -Pacific is not just an extensive region but also a 
strategic imaginary, through which states construct policy frameworks and rationalize other security arrangements 
(Beeson & Wilson, 2019). The regional construct has on its account the Indian Ocean, bringing energy transport 
channels, chokepoints, e.g., the Strait of Malacca and the increased significance of the Bay of Bengal in the 
projection of power (Kapoor, 2020; Brewster, 2020). 
Strategic Competition and Major-Power Rivalry 
Strategic competition between United States and China is the hallmark of the Indo-Pacific. The emergence of China 
as a maritime and economic force has complicated the regional system of the U.S., resu lting in a process of rivalry 
in the spheres of military, economic, and technology (Doshi, 2021). The Belt and Road Initiative, building dual -use 
ports, and the growth of the People Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) have now been seen as a wide effort to project  
influence down the so -called String of Pearls across the Indian Ocean (Pant & Joshi, 2020; Yoshihara & Holmes, 
2018). 
The United States has responded by stating its Free and Open Indo -Pacific (FOIP) strategy, putting priority on 
freedom of navigation, mar itime security, and safeguarding rules -based order (Green et al., 2019; Ratner, 2021). 
Such competition is not restricted to the military aspects; researchers suggest increasing importance of places that 
have been drawn between technology and economic stat ecraft, 5G networks, artificial intelligence, and trade 
alliances, as other metrics used in geoperational rivalry (Sullivan, 2021; Singh, 2021). Other reports refer to 
American and Chinese rivalry as a typical security dilemma situation, where one party defensive actions are seen as 
offensive ones by the other party (Koga, 2020). 
Alliance Structures and the Rise of Minilateralism 
Research Journal for Social Affairs, 03 (05) 2025. 503-520 
 
505 
 
Indo-Pacific can be described by a web of bilateral, trilateral, and multilateral security arrangements. In the past, the 
U.S. made its presence on the basis of the hub and spoke bilateral alliances with Japan, South Korea, Philippines, 
Australia, and Thailand (Smith, 2020). Nevertheless, the modern reality presents the increasing tendency at 
minilateralism, the establishment of small earmarked coalitions, which offer flexibility (Brewster, 2020). 
Minilateral cooperation is important and the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue (Quad), which has been revived in 
2017, is a cornerstone of it. The core areas of interest to the Quad are marit ime domain awareness, combined naval 
training such as Malabar, the security of supply chains, and new technologies (Schreer & Le Thu, 2021). Similarly, a 
new trilateral alliance like AUKUS which was instituted in 2021 represents a quantitative change of alliance politics 
with the promise to US, the provision of nuclear powered submarines and advanced technological cooperation of AI, 
cyber technology, and hypersonics to Australia (Grossman, 2021). The problem is that scholars state that these 
alliances are i ntended to discourage China without creating a formalized NATO -like institution in Asia 
(Parameswaran, 2020; Rapp-Hooper & Doshi, 2020). 
Regional Responses and Hedging Strategies 
Another very important aspect of Indo -Pacific geopolitics is the reaction of regional states, especially those in 
ASEAN and South Asia states. Most of these states engage in strategic hedging, that is, they combine economic 
relations with China and security partnership with the United States and its allies (Kuik, 2020; Chong, 2021) . As an 
example, Vietnam has strengthened the military relations with the U.S. but tries to be careful not to directly ally 
itself, and Indonesia has foreign policy focused on ASEAN centrality and non-alignment (Yeo, 2021). 
India is a special case of asymmetric alignment and independence. Its Act East Policy and the expansion of its navy 
in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands demonstrate that it is capable of negating China, but it does not embrace any 
formal alliances that are an impulsion of New Delhi given i ts traditional non -alignment (Pant & Joshi, 2020). 
Different middle powers such as South Korea and Australia respond to these pressures in different ways, and 
Australia has been tied deeper into U.S.-centered minilateral arrangements, but Seoul is more actors dealing with the 
Korean Peninsula, though agency initiative skeptical of general Indo-Pacific initiatives (Bhatia, 2021). 
Emerging Security Domains: Grey-Zone Tactics and Technology 
The modern literature emphasizes the fact of spreading of the competit ion to some nontraditional and grey -zone 
spheres. An example of China involved in incremental coercion is the deployment of coast guard vessels and 
maritime militia in the South China Sea that ultimately undermines the status quo without causing an open wa r 
(Poling, 2020). In parallel, cybersecurity, space, and artificial intelligence have emerged as the fields in which 
alliances should be formed, and Quad and AUKUS focused on technology sharing as one of the most powerful 
means of deterrence (Singh, 2021; Tan, 2021). 
The topic of infrastructure and securing the economy also comes up in the context of the new strategic calculus by 
scholars. The existence of rivalry in the development of connectivity, which has seen the entrance of the BRI, 
together with the Blue Dot Network led by the U.S. and Japan, illustrates how economic power has become an 
instrument of geopolitical jockeying (Grare, 2021). The Indo -Pacific can be viewed as a crucible of hybrid/ 
multidimensional power politics because of this convergence of conventional-style power politics and nontraditional 
spaces of hybrids. 
A number of perspectives are reached within the literature. To begin with, the Indo -Pacific was the hotbed of 
strategic competition in the 21 st century with the rivalry between th e United States and China being the major 
theme of strategic competition in military, economic as well as technological fields. Second, the politics of alliances 
are becoming more flexible and minilateral in the latest examples such as the Quad and AUKUS, supplementing 
rather than substituting conventional bilateral alliance systems. Third, states within a region use hedging and 
selective orientation as a means to keep their independence, and at the same time take advantage of both great 
powers. Lastly, the  increasing attention to the grey -zone methods, cyber space and economic power demonstrates 
that Indo-Pacific security goes beyond traditional military reasoning. This research approach is an extension of these 
ideas but in an attempt to consider the relat ionship between the strategic rivalry and alliance changes that in turn 
influence the security outcomes in a region. 
METHODOLOGY 
Research Design 
In this research, qualitative research design was used based upon the exploratory and descriptive approach because it 
had to look at evolving geopolitics in Indo -Pacific. The choice of qualitative method was due to the possibility of 
obtaining a well -informed insight into the intricate nature of politics and the political interactions and format of 
security in the region that could not be perceived through quantification indicators. The project was intended to 
examine how strategic rivalry among great powers, developments of alliances and minilateral structures, and 
reactions of the regional players influence the In do-Pacific security system. Lacking in the hypothesis testing, but 
Research Journal for Social Affairs, 03 (05) 2025. 503-520 
 
506 
 
emphasizing on the interpretative analysis, the research attempted to elicit subtle perspectives on the political, 
strategic, and economic peculiarities of the Indo-Pacific geopolitics. 
Data Sources 
Primary data directives were not used; instead, secondary data were used, such as a broad spectrum of scholarly 
work, policy documents and government reports and an assessment of thinks tanks. Theorizing, historical overlook, 
and regional securit y studies were revealed through scholarly studies in peer -reviewed journals, books, and edited 
volumes. The policy documents used were the United States Indo-Pacific Strategy (2022) and statements of the Act 
East Policy by India, and the ASEAN Outlook on t he Indo-Pacific (2019) to learn about the official stances and 
policies of key regional actors. Think tank reports and working papers on the security trends, alliance building and 
technological rivalry provided by the Australian Strategic Policy Institute (ASPI), Carnegie Endowment for 
International Peace, RAND Corporation, and Observer Research Foundation (ORF) were also included to capture 
the current estimate of security trends, alliance building and technological competition in the region. Analysis of 
media reports and official press releases of the U.S. Department of Defense, Japanese Ministry of Defense and 
Indian Ministry of External Affairs have also been considered to trace changing security discourses and reactions to 
security issues. 
Data Collection and Selection Criteria 
The literature selection involved a purposive sampling approach in suchway that literature selected had to be directly 
related to the three main dimensions of this study, namely strategic competition, alliance and minilateralism a nd 
regional security responses. Publications released in the years 2015 -2025 were more highly favored to ensure that 
the most up to date findings conveyed research findings and capture all the breakthroughs, especially the revival of 
the Quad, the establishment of the AUKUS, and the increased pace of competition between the U.S. and China. The 
historical selection was quite limited to give the background of the formation of the concept of the Indo -Pacific and 
the history of the U.S. bilateral alliance -oriented approach in Asia. Peer-reviewed journal articles were identified in 
academic databases, like Scopus, JSTOR, Taylor and Francis and Google Scholar, whereas government websites 
and websites of international organizations were consulted on primary documents and strategic white papers. 
Data Analysis 
The comprehensive data that was gathered then underwent the thematic analysis where the research was able to 
compartmentalize information into coherent analytical themes. These topics were: 1) strategic rivalry and great -
power competition, 2) the developments of alliances and minilateral patterns, and 3) the regional security processes 
and hedging. In each theme, we looked at the content within it to identify patterns, divergences and new trends. 
Qualitative content analysis methodology was applied to derive useful information and also how the empirical trends 
could be connected to theory as in the case of balance-of-power theory, security dilemma and alliance politics. Such 
an approach made it possible to determine how strategic behaviors of the U.S. and Ch inese apply to the regional 
states, developments in the reformation of alliances towards continuation of competition, and how smaller and 
middle powers employ the hedging or alignment tools. 
Triangulation was also taken into consideration in conducting the  analysis as a means of achieving credibility and 
robustness. The results of academic resources were also triangulated with policy articles and think tank reports to 
reduce the likelihood of biasness or overindulgence on a particular view. Preference was l aid on separating policy 
rhetoric with action, especially in matters relating to operationalization of AUKUS, maritime initiatives of the Quad 
and ASEAN centrality attempts. 
Ethical Considerations 
However, since all of the research was conducted based sole ly on secondary sources together with open -source

Main argument: The Indo-Pacific is the central arena of 21st-century great power competition, characterized by intensified U.S.-China rivalry, evolving minilateral alliances, and emerging regional security challenges including non-traditional threats.

Research design: Qualitative exploratory and descriptive design using thematic content analysis of academic literature, policy documents, think tank publications, and official statements.

Method: Qualitative thematic content analysis combined with triangulation of diverse secondary sources to identify trends in strategic rivalry, alliances, and regional security responses.

Dataset or evidence: Secondary data from peer-reviewed journals, policy papers (U.S. Indo-Pacific Strategy, ASEAN Outlook), think tank reports (ASPI, Carnegie, RAND, ORF), and official government press releases from U.S., Japan, and India.

Unit of analysis: The Indo-Pacific region as a geopolitical and security construct, focusing on great powers (U.S., China), minilateral alliances (Quad, AUKUS), and regional middle powers' responses.

Time period studied: Primarily 2015 to 2025, focusing on recent developments such as Quad revival and AUKUS formation.

Geographic focus: Indo-Pacific region spanning from eastern Africa through the Indian Ocean to the western Pacific, with attention to South China Sea, Strait of Malacca, and related maritime domains.

Identification strategy: Thematic analysis of diverse secondary sources with purposive sampling; triangulation to corroborate findings and distinguish rhetoric from operational realities.

title: The US strategy of multidomain containment and China’s counter-responses in the Indo-Pacific (2019–2025)
abstract: Type of the article: Research articleThe intensifying United States-China rivalry in the Indo-Pacific has gained acute relevance for global order as strategic competition extends across military, technological, economic, and cognitive domains. This paper examines the extent and modalities of the US multidimensional strategic encirclement of China in the Indo-Pacific and analyzes China’s multidomain responses, including the PLA’s intelligentization, technological sovereignty initiatives, and economic re-sovereignization, over the period 2019–2025. The study adopts a qualitative interpretivist methodology, drawing on scholarly and primary sources, including defense doctrines, alliance frameworks such as AUKUS and QUAD, legislative instruments, and multilingual Chinese perspectives. The analysis shows that the US employs layered alliance-building, technology governance through semiconductor and export-control regimes, triangulated partnerships with actors such as Israel and India, and selective interventions in regional states, including Pakistan and the Philippines, to constrain Chinese influence. China’s countermeasures are multidimensional: advancing AI-enabled military modernization, securing strategic port access at Gwadar, Hambantota, and Ream, and reinforcing economic insulation through its Dual Circulation Strategy and yuan-based energy agreements. Results indicate that encirclement is no longer limited to geography but increasingly embedded in digital infrastructure, economic flows, and cognitive influence. The study concludes that these dynamics are accelerating a shift toward bifurcated multipolarity, marked by competing techno-security ecosystems and divergent governance norms, with significant implications for alliance cohesion, technological sovereignty, and the management of strategic escalation.Acknowledgments I would like to express my sincere gratitude to my teachers and academic peers whose valuable insights, encouragement, and constructive discussions inspire me to enrich the quality of my work. I am especially indebted to my family – my wife and children – for their patience, understanding, and unwavering support during the long hours of research and writing. Their endurance and encouragement made this endeavor possible.

nance through semiconductor and export-control regimes, triangulated partnerships

INTRODUCTION
The rivalry between the United States and China in the Indo-Pacific 
has intensified into a multidomain contest that transcends tradi -
tional military confrontation. Since 2019, the Indo-Pacific has be -
come the principal arena in which the US seeks to operationalize a 
strategy of multidomain containment – integrating military deter -
rence, technological restrictions, economic coalitions, and norm a-
tive influence – to circumscribe China’s rise. The central pro blem 
that emerges is how this strategic encirclement is being constructed 
across multiple domains simultaneously, and to what extent it is re-
shaping the systemic balance of power. Rather than being confined 
to conventional geopolitical competition, the confrontation now e x-
tends into semiconductor supply chains, artificial intellige nce gover-
nance, alliance architectures, and the regulation of digital and eco -
nomic ecosystems.

This evolution creates a complex scientific problem for the study of international relations: understand-
ing how multidomain containment strategies are conceptualized and executed by a hegemon in relative 
decline, and how a rising power formulates adaptive counter-response s. Existing scholarship has ad -
dressed US hegemonic retrenchment (Ikenberry, 2008) and China’s ascent (Shambaugh, 2013), yet these 
works often isolate military deterrence from techno-economic rival ry or focus narrowly on decoupling 
debates. Such fragmentation obscures the interdependence of domains in which the rivalry unfolds and 
risks oversimplifying China’s strategic posture as merely reactiv e. The absence of an integrated, multi -
domain framework has resulted in blind spots in both policy assessment and aca demic analysis.
The problem under investigation, therefore, lies in the insufficiently theorized and empirically underde-
veloped understanding of how multidomain containment and counter-c ontainment strategies interact 
in real time in the Indo-Pacific between 2019 and 2025 (data collection cut- off: July 2025). Specifically, 
the challenge is to explain how alliance-building, doctrinal innovat ion, and indigenous technological 
development are mobilized in response to simultaneous pressures acro ss the military, economic, and 
technological theatres of competition. Addressing this problem is c rucial, as the period 2024–2025 has 
witnessed unprecedented intensification of semiconductor choke point strategies, artificial intelligence 
governance initiatives, and alliance expansion, all of which carry si gnificant implications for the future 
architecture of global order.
1. LITERATURE REVIEW
Scholarship on the US-China rivalry in the Indo-
Pacific has proliferated across several strands of 
international relations theory, yet remains frag -
mented in scope and integration. Three broad 
traditions – neorealism, offensive realism, and 
complex interdependence theory – provide the 
dominant conceptual frames for understand-
ing the dynamics of containment and counter-
containment. Neorealist scholarship highlights 
how systemic anarchy compels the US to engage 
in external balancing through alliance forma -
tion and forward deployment, a trend visible in 
AUKUS, the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue 
(QUAD), and renewed bilateral defense agree -
ments with India and Japan. These institution -
alized forms of balancing underscore how sys -
temic pressures generate collective responses to 
China’s rise. Building upon this, offensive real -
ism emphasizes the pursuit of regional hegemo -
ny: China’s assertive posture in the South China 
Sea, its Belt and Road Initiative, and its acceler-
ated military modernization are interpreted as 
steps toward displacing US primacy. US poli -
cies such as the 2022 Indo-Pacific Strategy (The 
White House, 2022) and the CHIPS and Science 
Act (Legislation of United States, 2022), which 
constrain Chinese technological growth, reflect 
pre-emptive containment measures rooted in 
hegemonic rivalry.
At the same time, realist interpretations are insuf -
ficient without recognition of economic and tech -
nological interdependence. Complex interdepen -
dence theory (Keohane & Nye, 1977) complicates 
zero-sum portrayals by illustrating how semicon -
ductor supply chains, rare earth dependencies, 
and cross-border financial flows bind the two ri -
vals even as these ties are weaponized. Export con-
trols imposed by Washington in 2022 and Beijing’s 
restrictions on gallium and germanium in 2023 
exemplify how interdependence has shifted from 
stabilizing linkage to a coercive instrument. The 
literature thus underscores a paradox: interdepen-
dence that once moderated conflict is now a con -
tested arena of statecraft.
Western scholarship has made substantial con -
tributions to theorizing this rivalry. Ikenberry 
(2008) and Friedberg (2011) conceptualize the 
Indo-Pacific contest as part of a liberal order un -
der stress, while Mearsheimer (2001) emphasizes 
the intensifying security dilemma. Recent analy -
ses highlight the convergence of deterrence and 
techno-economic denial (Glaser, 2015; Campbell 
& Doshi, 2025, yet often depict China as reactive 
rather than proactive. This tendency overlooks 
doctrinal developments such as the PLA’s intelli -
gentized warfare guidelines. Intelligentization  is 
an advanced integration of artificial intelligence, 
machine learning, data analytics, and cognitive 
computing into systems and structures, enabling 
47
Geopolitics under Globalization,  Volume 6, 2025
https://doi.org/10.21511/gg.06(1).2025.05
autonomous, adaptive, and intelligent opera -
tions that surpass traditional automation (Pan et 
al., 2024; State Council Information Office, 2019; 
Tellis, 2025), which frame technological inno -
vation as central to China’s strategic autonomy. 
Moreover, thematic compartmentalization per -
sists: works on military deterrence (Shambaugh, 
2013), economic decoupling (Baldwin, 2020), and 
technological bifurcation (Segal, 2016) remain an-
alytically siloed, obscuring the multidomain char -
acter of US containment.
Non-Western perspectives provide a more holistic 
understanding of the rivalry. Chinese scholarship, 
particularly through concepts such as major pow -
er diplomacy ( 大国外交), community of shared 
destiny ( 命运共同体), and intelligentized war -
fare (智能化战争), frames China’s rise as restor -
ative rather than revisionist. Yan Xuetong’s moral 
realism situates Chinese strategy in Confucian 
traditions and the tianxia worldview, while Liu 
Mingfu’s China Dream articulates a technologi -
cally empowered national rejuvenation. Regional 
voices from ASEAN emphasize inclusive order-
building, with the ASEAN Outlook on the Indo-
Pacific (ASEAN, 2019) rejecting zero-sum for -
mulations. Singh and Marwah (2023) interpret 
China’s outreach as pragmatic balancing against 
what they perceive as Western conditionality. 
Similarly, national strategies from Japan, South 
Korea, India, and Australia reveal nuanced posi -
tions – ranging from Japan’s prioritization of AI 
and space security, to South Korea’s hedging be -
tween alliance commitments and economic ties, 
to India’s dual posture of alignment through the 
QUAD and strategic autonomy, and to Australia’s 
concern with “grey zone” coercion. The European 
Union, meanwhile, has advanced a normative 
Indo-Pacific agenda, with France and Germany 
participating in freedom of navigation operations 
(EU, 2021).
Across these literatures, three enduring contra -
dictions emerge. First, the stability–vulnerability 
paradox of interdependence highlights whether 
economic entanglement reduces or amplifies con-
flict risks. Second, competing interpretations of 
China’s intent divide the field: Western analyses 
tend to cast China as revisionist, whereas Chinese 
and some ASEAN perspectives emphasize restor -
ative and non-expansionist logics. Third, debates 
persist over whether military deterrence or tech -
no-economic leverage constitutes the primary are-
na of competition, with recent developments in AI 
governance and semiconductor control suggesting 
that the boundaries between the two are increas -
ingly blurred.
This review highlights the need for an integrated 
framework that synthesizes realist power-balanc -
ing, interdependence dynamics, and non-Western 
strategic thought. Existing studies, while rich in 
detail, often remain compartmentalized and epis -
temically asymmetric, privileging Western sourc -
es at the expense of Chinese primary materials. 
This study seeks to address these gaps by combin -
ing neorealism, offensive realism, and complex in-
terdependence with multilingual primary sources 
and underutilized Chinese strategic doctrines. In 
doing so, it contributes to a more comprehensive 
understanding of US multidomain containment 
and China’s counter-responses in the Indo-Pacific 
between 2019 and 2025, positioning this rivalry 
not merely as a geopolitical struggle but as a mul -
tidimensional contest over technology, alliances, 
and systemic order.
2. METHODS 
This study adopts a qualitative interpretive design 
to examine the dynamics of US multidomain con-
tainment and China’s counter-responses in the 
Indo-Pacific during the 2019 to 2025. The meth -
odological approach is structured in three stages: 
(1) corpus assembly, (2) data processing and cod -
ing, and (3) interpretive analysis.
2.1. Corpus assembly
The data set was purposively compiled to cap -
ture official strategy documents, legislative acts, 
alliance communiqués, peer-reviewed scholar -
ship, think tank reports, and reputable media 
analyses in both English and Chinese. Primary 
materials include China’s Defence White Papers 
(2020, 2023), the US Indo-Pacific Strategy (The 
White House, 2022), NATO Strategic Concepts 
(Vilnius 2022–2024), AUKUS and QUAD state -
ments, the CHIPS and Science Act, and policy 
papers from the Ministries of Foreign Affairs 
and Defence in China, the United States, and al -
48
Geopolitics under Globalization,  Volume 6, 2025
https://doi.org/10.21511/gg.06(1).2025.05
lied states. Supplementary sources were drawn 
from think tanks (e.g., CSIS, CNAS, Carnegie, 
Brookings; CIIS, SIIS, China Strategic Culture 
Promotion Association), peer-reviewed journals 
(International Security, China Quarterly, Foreign 
Affairs), and major regional and global media out-
lets (e.g., South China Morning Post, Financial 
Times, Global Times). Chinese-language docu -
ments were retrieved from PLA Daily ( 解放军报 
[pinyin: Jiěfàngjūn Bào] ), Xinhua, and academic 
journals from institutions such as Renmin and 
Tsinghua Universities.
2.2. Data processing and coding
All textual data were imported into NVivo and 
Atlas.ti for thematic coding. An inductive code-
book was developed through open coding, followed 
by axial coding to identify cross-domain clusters, 
such as “containment,” “counter-containment,” 
“techno-sovereignty,” and “interdependence.” Co-
occurrence analysis was applied to detect relation-
ships between military, technological, and econom-
ic strategies. To ensure reliability, Chinese-language 
materials were processed through a two-stage pro-
cess to ensure both linguistic accuracy and concep-
tual fidelity. First, source texts were processed on 
encrypted, offline translation software, prevent -
ing any exposure of sensitive material to external 
servers. Second, translations were reviewed and 
refined by bilingual researchers with graduate-
level proficiency (C1 CEFR or equivalent) in the 
relevant languages and formal training in interna-
tional relations and security studies. For example, 
the Chinese doctrinal term “智能化战争” (zhìnéng 
huà zhànzhēng) was translated as “intelligentized 
warfare.” The alternatives such as “intelligent war-
fare” or “AI-enabled warfare,” were considered but 
retained “intelligentized warfare” to align with ter-
minology used in the People’s Liberation Army’s 
own white papers. 
2.3. Interpretive analysis
The study is grounded in constructivist episte -
mology, treating international strategy as socially 
constructed and ideologically framed. This inter -
pretive framework allows doctrinal statements, 
alliance structures, and policy narratives to be 
read not only as material instruments but also as 
discursive practices. The method complements 
the study’s theoretical synthesis of neorealism, of -
fensive realism, and complex interdependence, 
enabling analysis of both structural drivers (e.g., 
alliance-building, deterrence) and normative 
worldviews (e.g., “major power diplomacy,” “intel-
ligentized warfare”).
2.4. Ethical and practical 
considerations
All materials were derived from open-source and 
publicly available documents. The study follows 
COPE guidelines (2023), GDPR provisions, and 
China’s Personal Information Protection Law 
(2021). Personal identifiers in social media or com-
mentary sources were removed or anonymized. 
No IRB approval was required, as the study in -
volved no direct interaction with human partici -
pants. Where classified materials were unavail -
able, findings were triangulated with declassified 
documents, open-source intelligence (OSINT), 
and expert symposia. Interpretive neutrality was 
maintained through cross-checking ideologically 
divergent sources (e.g., Global Times vs. CSIS).
3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
This study examined the modalities of the United 
States’ multidomain containment strategy in the 
Indo-Pacific and China’s counter-responses be -
tween 2019 and 2025. Using interpretive thematic 
coding of multilingual primary and secondary 
sources, the findings reveal a layered and asym -
metrical rivalry unfolding across military, tech -
nological, economic, and ideational domains. This 
section integrates empirical results (Tables 1-8; 
Figures 1-2) with theoretical interpretation, there-
by situating the evidence within the hybrid frame-
work of neorealism, offensive realism, and com -
plex interdependence.
3.1. US encircling China
The data confirm that Washington’s strategy oper-
ates as a strategic mesh (Table 1), comprising over-
lapping alliances (AUKUS, QUAD, JAPHUS, NATO 
outreach) and techno-security nodes. This modular 
network is consistent with Mearsheimer’s offensive 
realism, which highlights the creation of redundant 
balancing mechanisms against rising challengers. 
49
Geopolitics under Globalization,  Volume 6, 2025
https://doi.org/10.21511/gg.06(1).2025.05
These networked frameworks follow what 
Mearsheimer (2001) would term offensive real -
ism in modular alliance formation, where the US 
hedges against China’s rise by building overlap -
ping technological and military dependencies in 
regions adjacent to China’s core maritime corri -
dors (e.g., South and East China Seas).
Yet, complex interdependence is also evident: 
India and Israel serve as intermediary hubs for 
technology transfers (Table 2), allowing the US to 
shape Asia’s defense ecosystem without triggering 
overt escalation.
These transfers align with the dual logic of real -
ist containment and neoliberal interdependence, 
whereby US retains control over core components 
while leveraging allied national champions to 
populate Asia’s defense-technological ecosystem.
NATO’s 2024 Vilnius Summit marks a notable se-
mantic shift in the Alliance’s doctrinal perimeter. 
By explicitly labelling China a “systemic challenge,” 
NATO moves beyond its traditional Atlantic focus, 
signalling a doctrinal convergence between Euro-
Atlantic and Indo-Pacific strategies (NATO, 2024). 
This evolution supports the argument that the en -
circlement is not just regional but systemic.
Western scholars often interpret this shift as ideo-
logical – liberal democracies reacting to authori -
tarian assertiveness (Ikenberry, 2008). However,
