2 Who Reviews Whom, Where, and Why? 
among states. One prominent tool is the peer review sys- 
tem hosted by international organizations (IOs). Peer re- 
views can be found across issue areas as diverse as the envi- 
ronment, ﬁnance, development, security, and human rights. 
While they can take different forms, such reviews always en- 
tail the evaluation of the practice and performance of a state 
by other states. Contrary to coercive modes of governance, 
peer reviews are “soft governance” instruments that seek to 
induce states to comply with the standards touted by IOs 
(e.g., Pagani 2002 ; Lehtonen 2007 ; Liverani and Lundgren 
2007 ; Carraro, Conzelmann, and Jongen 2019 ). 
The existing literature on peer reviews in world politics 
has largely focused on their effectiveness, suggesting that 
they can inﬂuence state behavior through several possible 
mechanisms. Some have argued that peer reviews affect 
change through policy learning ( Marcussen 2003 ; Lehtonen 
2007 ; Mahon and McBride 2009 ). Others suggest that re- 
views incentivize compliance by informing an international 
audience about the extent to which states conform with 
agreed-upon standards ( Terman and Voeten 2018 ). Nega- 
tive assessments can hurt the reputation of states and this, in 
turn, mobilizes domestic actors to pressure governments to 
change their ways ( Carraro 2019 ). Others again understand 
states as social creatures that care about the approval of their 
peers, and thus work to receive positive reviews and avoid 
reputational damage ( Carraro, Conzelmann, and Jongen 
2019 ). Akin to global performance indicators, peer reviews 
establish a framework for comparability among states that 
reveal shortcomings and thus serve as instruments of so- 
cial pressure: Because laggards of performance can easily 
be identiﬁed, these rankings induce states to improve their 
practices (e.g., Kelley and Simmons 2015 ; Koliev, Sommerer, 
and Tallberg 2020 ). 
If negative assessments can be costly for states, it is plau- 
sible that states might act to inﬂuence aspects of the peer 
review process that could increase the chances of a posi- 
tive assessment. Indeed, recent work by Terman and Voeten 
(2018 ) shows that strategic relations among states affect 
peer review assessments in the United Nations Universal 
Periodic Review: Examiner countries that evaluate partners 
tend to be less critical in evaluating their human rights 
records than they are vis-à-vis countries with whom they do 
not share strategic relations. Such a pattern provides evi- 
dence of politics inﬁltrating the peer review process and 
raises the stakes of assignment decisions about who gets re- 
viewed by whom, how, and where—a  decision that, thus far, 
scholars have implicitly assumed to be largely process-driven 
and impartial. If states themselves were indeed able to in- 
ﬂuence assignment decisions, then politics might enter the 
peer review process well before more or less favorable re- 
views are written. Such a possibility would have implications 
for inferences that scholars draw when assessing state com- 
pliance with peer review recommendations. 
Although peer review tools are often portrayed as exam- 
ples of relational governance, with states evaluating other 
states, their credibility rests on the consistent deployment of 
a comparable methodology ( Jongen 2018 ). Typically, this in- 
cludes explicit IO guidance on how to conduct the peer re- 
view process, including self-assessments, reporting, and pub- 
lication requirements. While member states need to broadly 
agree on the mechanics of such a process, it is in the purview 
of IO secretariats to devise standard procedures and subse- 
quently ensure that they are followed. In this paper, we as- 
sess the extent to which review assignment decisions are in- 
deed impartial and independent, or whether they are politi- 
cized. 
We tackle this question by using the Organization for Eco- 
nomic Cooperation and Development (OECD) Develop- 
ment Assistance Committee’s (DAC) peer review system as 
our empirical case. We consider the OECD DAC a relevant 
laboratory for three reasons: First, the DAC has the longest- 
standing system of peer evaluation within the OECD, with 
a total of over 500 reviews between 1962 and 2020. Second, 
while previous research has recognized the role of the DAC 
peer review in advancing best practices among donor coun- 
tries in international development cooperation ( Liverani 
and Lundgren 2007 ; Paulo and Reisen 2010 ; Ashoff 2013 ; 
Eyben 2013 ), little attention has been paid to how this sys- 
tem works and how it shapes states’ aid policies and prac- 
tices. Third, the foreign aid literature has produced robust 
evidence documenting that donor strategic interests mat- 
ter in foreign aid decision-making (e.g., Alesina and Dollar 
2000 ; Heinrich 2013 ; Bermeo 2017 ). Also, there is evidence 
suggesting that donor political economies yield divergent 
preferences about how donors want to promote develop- 
ment abroad ( Dietrich 2016 , 2021 ; Dietrich, Reinsberg, and 
Steinwand 2022 ). If states can expect more favorable reviews 
from peers that are strategically or ideologically aligned with 
them, they might lobby the Secretariat to grant them condi- 
tions for more favorable assessments. 1 
Drawing on extensive research on organizational pro- 
cesses in the OECD Secretariat, we develop a theoretical 
framework that focuses on the role of the IO secretariats 
as stewards of the peer review methodology. Given their 
rational-legal authority, IO secretariats are uniquely posi- 
tioned to assume this role ( Barnett and Finnemore 1999 ). 
We develop a bureaucratic process model that features 
mandate-driven criteria and that, if implemented correctly 
and consistently, should ensure that assignment decisions 
are impartial and independent of state interests. We then 
augment the bureaucratic process model with factors that 
reﬂect particularistic donor interests and that could be ex- 
pected to affect assignment decisions made by the OECD 
Secretariat. In a ﬁrst step, we use this approach to explain 
decisions about who reviews whom—i.e.,  which DAC mem- 
ber states serve as peer examiners for a particular review. In 
a second step, we explain the choice of which aid recipient 
countries will be visited during the review to examine the 
reviewed donor’s practices in-depth.

title: Aviation exceptionalism, fossil fuels and the state
abstract: While states have accelerated the energy transition in some sectors, they have also obstructed fossil phase-out in other sectors. Aviation has an outsized and rapidly growing climate impact, and associated policy decisions have perpetuated fossil fuel use. Since aviation is dependent on high energy density that only fossil fuels can (currently) provide, the industry faces fundamental constraints to green its capital. Yet, the industry does not operate in isolation. In this paper, we show how the state performs a variety of roles that benefit from and support aviation, creating conflicts with the state’s climate targets. We analyze state–industry relations as they relate to the emergence of air transport and its ongoing carbon-dependent formulations. Combining a relational account of the state and the method of critical problem-solving, we characterize the roles of the state vis-à-vis the industry as owner, sponsor and customer and point to strategies of how the associated capacities can be leveraged to drive fossil phase-out in aviation. Since a rapid and comprehensive phase-out of fossil fuels is required for climate stabilization, we argue that political economists can make important contributions by focusing on the socio-material relations that constrain state agency to phase-out fossil fuels in specific sectors.

title: NATO in Kosovo and the logic of successful security practices
abstract: Abstract NATO's involvement in Kosovo and its transformation from a military intervention to a UN-authorized peacekeeping operation has played a key role in the evolution of the alliance's strategic and political agenda. This article explores the importance of NATO's engagement with Kosovo in retrospect and in relation to the future outlook for European and global peace and security. It focuses on the centrality of this case for NATO's post-Cold War identity and as a key issue in the renewed political conflict associated with the transitional international order. We make three arguments. First, we argue that NATO's involvement in Kosovo has shaped and exacerbated the broader friction associated with the shifting international order. Second, we make the case that this engagement has played a key role in the strategic, political and operational development of NATO and its evolving identity. Thirdly, as a result of this, we argue that NATO's evolution and transformation in Kosovo was guided by what we call the logic of successful security practices. This entails making prudent political choices and implementing practical steps to harmonize divergent strategic interests among NATO members, adapting to shifting security circumstances, and upholding the organization's significance, credibility and influence both within and beyond the Euro-Atlantic community.

NATO in Kosovo and the logic of 
successful security practices
EDWARD NEWMAN AND GËZIM VISOKA *
International Affairs 100: 2 (2024) 631–653; doi: 10.1093/ia/iiae014

The momentous events that occurred in Kosovo in 1999 and their international 
repercussions arguably make that year a watershed both for NATO’s post-Cold War 
evolution and for the transitional international order. NATO’s military operations 
in Kosovo and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, undertaken without the direct 
authorization of the United Nations Security Council (UNSC), were ostensibly 
aimed at ending and preventing egregious human rights abuses, but this narra-
tive remains highly controversial.1 The subsequent UN administration of Kosovo 
facilitated its path to independent statehood, albeit without universal recogni-
tion. NATO’s intervention brought into focus some of the defining international 
challenges of the post-Cold War era, and it continues to shape the geopolitical 
and normative friction and contestation which destabilize international politics.
This article explores NATO’s engagement with Kosovo in retrospect and in 
relation to the future outlook for European and global peace and security. W e 
seek to understand what explains NATO’s involvement and the evolution of its 
security practices in Kosovo and how this engagement has shaped its strategic and 
global relations. Drawing on practice theory, we offer a novel interpretation of the 
logic of NATO’s involvement and transformation in Kosovo. NATO’s evolution 
and transformation in Kosovo were guided by what we call the ‘logic of successful 
security practices’. W e define this as the political decisions and practical actions 
that are designed to reconcile the diverse interests of NATO’s member states, 
the host authorities and other challenging forces. The logic of successful security 
practices aims to engage with the divergent strategic interests of its members and 
respond to the changing security environment, while ensuring that the organiza-
tion retains its relevance, legitimacy and role within and beyond the Euro-Atlantic 
community.2 It is a core feature of NATO’s quest for cohesion as a ‘polycentric’ 
alliance and contested global security actor.3

by Tracey German and Andrew Dorman.

At the strategic level, NATO’s involvement in Kosovo has undoubtedly shaped 
and exacerbated the broader friction associated with the shifting international 
order, and has played a key role in the strategic, political and operational develop-
ment of NATO and its evolving identity. This theme has received close attention 
in the past, 4 but it has attracted renewed urgency and significance since 2022 in the 
context of heightened geopolitical conflict, including the broader impact of the 
Ukraine war. This provides a compelling case for revisiting this challenge. In turn, 
NATO’s ongoing engagement with Kosovo has not only generated friction but 
has also shaped the norms and institutions of international order. As a contested 
case of human protection, the ‘illegal but legitimate’ humanitarian interven-
tion of 1999 was undertaken without UNSC authorization, but had a significant 
degree of support within western societies and other parts of the ‘liberal bloc’. 5 
NATO’s intervention proved to be pivotal for a re-evaluation of if, when and how 
military force should be used to prevent or stop serious human rights abuse. The 
Responsibility to Protect (R2P) principle, agreed by all UN members in 2005, 
is a central part of this legacy, 6 but so too is the controversy surrounding the 
Kosovo intervention, which is viewed outside western circles as a demonstration 
of hegemony and an abuse of power, which exposed the geopolitical polarization 
that has become increasingly acute in the twenty-first century.
The forms of NATO’s engagement with Kosovo—in terms of humanitarian 
intervention, the recognition of a de facto state and the expansion of NATO’s 
sphere of operations—remain active subjects of controversy as the relative balance 
of power and influence in international relations shifts. 7 NATO’s controversial 
intervention in Kosovo and its role in Kosovo’s disputed independence were in 
many ways a demonstration of the ‘unipolar moment’—the heyday of post-Cold 
War liberal internationalism. This engagement exposed divisions with respect to 
norms related to human rights, international recognition, territorial integrity and 
state sovereignty, and also in terms of the relationship between the western liberal 
alliance and the rising and resurgent non-liberal powers in the context of a shift 
towards multipolarity. This has put NATO at the heart of a fractious political 
conflict about the norms and institutions which define international order: where 
they come from, who leads and sponsors them, and who is represented in the 
organizations which administer and uphold them. 8 NATO’s engagement with

Kosovo has therefore made the country a focal point for broader political rivalry 
between some western supporters which promote the idea of a resurgent liber -
alism in international relations, and rising powers which seek to contest western 
power and influence. 9 The Ukraine war has exacerbated this; as Minister of 
Foreign Affairs of the Russian Federation Sergey Lavrov suggested, any solution 
to that conflict must focus on creating a ‘new world order’ which is detached from 
United States hegemony. 10
At the operational level, NATO’s intervention and engagement with Kosovo 
helped to forge a reinvented vision for the alliance orientated around new political 
and military challenges, as the post-Cold War ‘honeymoon’ gave way to renewed 
geopolitical friction. During the 1990s, an era defined by liberal internationalism 
under the hegemony of the US, the role and relevance of NATO had come into 
question. 11 Kosovo injected momentum and new relevance into the transforma-
tion of NATO’s security and crisis response apparatus, and its political mission. 
In some areas this activity has defined the practices and challenges of interna-
tional stabilization: Kosovo was a key case of international administration and 
post-conflict peacebuilding that has informed debates about the challenges, ethics 
and controversies of major interventions aimed at building or rebuilding institu-
tions and peace following armed conflict. 12 The alliance embraced and promoted 
the widening and deepening security agenda, and an operational focus on stabili-
zation and conflict prevention, effectively moving NATO into the humanitarian 
space. NATO’s approach to peacekeeping in Kosovo and the proclaimed success 
have been by-products of a repertoire of practices assembled in conjunction with 
other international missions in Kosovo, as well as broader political, legal and social 
discourses and events which shaped the meaning of security, statehood and the 
role of international community in Kosovo.
W e argue that NATO’s broad mandate to maintain safety and security in 
Kosovo was essential to its successful security practices. This mandate allowed 
the NATO-led Kosovo Force (KFOR) to change its mission and strategy in 
Kosovo and transform itself into a multifaceted operation capable of preventing, 
mitigating and transforming conflicts through diplomatic, political and military 
means. In this sense, NATO in the post-Cold War era is a quintessential case of 
organizational adaptation and strategic evolution with far-reaching repercussions 
for European and global peace and security. 13 Kosovo has been the incubator where 
NATO has shifted from a defence alliance into a multinational peacekeeping force

with partnerships with the European Union, the UN and the Organization for 
Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE). In particular, Kosovo has helped 
NATO take a multifaceted approach by adopting the UN’s peacekeeping princi-
ples of neutrality and impartiality, the EU’s diplomatic ambiguity with regard to 
Kosovo’s political status, and the conflict management tactics of other regional 
organizations.
Organized around the above themes, this article proceeds as follows. In the 
first part it examines the two phases of NATO’s quest for performing successful 
security practices in Kosovo, focusing on its transformation from humanitarian 
intervention to UN-authorized peacekeeping. In the second part, the article 
explores the legacy of NATO’s engagement in Kosovo for international norms 
related to intervention, secession and peacekeeping in contested states. It then 
concludes by exploring the implications of this case for NATO in the context of 
renewed great power geopolitical rivalry. This article relies on an analysis of the 
NATO-related literature, policy documents and other sources which capture both 
the discursive as well as the praxiological aspects of NATO’s role in Kosovo and 
its implications for adaptation in the transitional international order. Conceptu-
ally, the article draws on practice theory and constructivist security perspectives 
to develop the argument about the role of the logic of successful security practice 
in shaping NATO’s involvement in Kosovo.
NATO and the logic of successful security practices
NATO’s engagement in the western Balkans has been subject to wide discussion in 
security studies and international affairs. As the discourse and practice of security 
have constantly changed, so has the conceptual lens through which the practices 
of states and collective alliances and organizations are studied. 14 Yet, we still have 
an incomplete account of NATO’s involvement in Kosovo and its shift from a 
military intervention—considered widely as legitimate but legally flawed—to a 
UN-authorized peacekeeping mission. Realist and strategic studies scholars have 
interpreted NATO’s involvement in the region from a geopolitical perspective, 
exploring power projection, alliance politics and the primacy of the security of 
NATO members. Liberal scholars have considered NATO’s strategic expansion 
as crucial for safeguarding the liberal international order and for complementing 
the efforts of the UN in maintaining regional peace and stability. NATO thus 
provides benefits for its members, not only through the collective defence clause 
but also indirectly in advancing economic, diplomatic and political interests. 
Liberal institutionalists have focused on the institutionalist ‘stickiness’ that organi-
zations such as NATO develop over time, where path dependency and adaptive 
learning determine the endurance of such organizations. 15 This evolution also 
provides a platform for maintaining intra-alliance peace (for example between

and New York: Routledge, 2015).

Turkey and Greece) and reduces external hybrid threats (as in the case of NATO’s 
newest members, Montenegro and North Macedonia).
Normative scholars have approached NATO’s engagement with Kosovo both 
from the perspective of a challenge to international law, given the circumvention of 
the UNSC in relation to the intervention, and from the perspective of upholding 
humanitarian norms, such as the protection of civilians and the prevention of 
atrocities. Constructivists have highlighted the changing referents of security and 
provided an explanation for NATO’s fusion of kinetic and non-kinetic security 
as well as for the diffusion of territorial defence and human security. 16 They also 
question the normative justification for intervention and the norms and practices 
which have guided the doctrinal and operational aspects of NATO’s involvement 
in out-of-area situations.
While there are many interpretations as to how NATO evolved and changed 
to fit the post-Cold War international system, all agree that NATO’s goal is to 
maintain its relevance in relation to both its internal structures and members as 
well as the external environment, which includes rivals and transnational threats. 17 
NATO, as with any other military alliance, is prone to justifying its existence 
through the production of positive and successful results that benefit its members 
and improve its standing. In other words, it is only through tracing discursive and 
performative practice that we can make sense of NATO’s security logics and its 
transformation over time. 18 Putting the emphasis on practice is crucial, as it helps 
explain how actors or organizations interact, generate knowledge, implement 
rules, interpret norms and create symbolic orders of power. Practices, according 
to Adler, are ‘knowledge-constituted, meaningful patterns of socially recognized 
activity embedded in communities, routines, and organizations that structure 
experience’. 19 As Græger shows, from the perspective of practice theory ‘agents 
develop specific dispositions for acting and thinking in a particular way that is not 
based on a logic of consequences (instrumental), a logic of appropriateness (rule 
based), or a logic of rhetoric (communicative), but on a logic of practicality’. 20
In particular, practice theory shows how social interactions and shared knowl-
edge create communities of practice which configure their fluid actions, commit-
ments and relationships. Such situated networks, and such meaningful patterns of 
routines, play a crucial role in shaping the response of actors and organizations to 
different events and situations. As Adler and Pouliot argue, practices are formed as 
a result of ‘instances … of formative interactions’ which are due to ‘either material

title: Disinformation, deterrence and the politics of attribution
abstract: Abstract This article unpacks the politics of disinformation attribution as deterrence. Research and policy on disinformation deterrence commonly draw on frameworks inspired by cyber deterrence to address the ‘attribution problem’, thereby overlooking the political aspects underpinning attribution strategies in liberal democracies. Addressing this gap and bringing together disinformation studies and the fourth wave of deterrence theory, the article examines how acts of attribution serve liberal states' attempts at deterring foreign influence operations. In liberal states, disinformation as an external threat intersects with essential processes of public deliberation, and acts of attribution are charged with political risk. Introducing the concept of the ‘uncertainty loop’, the article demonstrates how the flow of uncertainty charges the decision-making situation in disinformation attribution. Drawing on three contemporary empirical cases—interference in the US presidential election of 2016, the Bundestag election in Germany in 2021 and the EU response to the COVID-19 ‘infodemic’ which erupted in 2020, the article illustrates how diverse strategies of attribution, non-attribution and diffused attribution have been navigated by governments. By laying bare the politics of disinformation attribution and advancing a conceptual apparatus for understanding its variations, the article expands current knowledge on disinformation deterrence and speaks to a broader International Relations literature on how deterrence strategies are mediated through political contexts.
main_argument: Disinformation attribution is a politically charged act in liberal democracies that functions as a form of deterrence by shaping how states respond to foreign influence operations, influenced by uncertainty and political risks.
research_design: Comparative qualitative analysis of three contemporary cases of disinformation attribution in liberal democracies.
dataset_or_evidence: Empirical examination of disinformation attribution strategies in the 2016 US presidential election, 2021 German Bundestag election, and the EU's response to the 2020 COVID-19 infodemic.

time_period_studied: 2016 to 2021, with focus on incidents occurring between 2016 and 2020.
geographic_focus: Liberal democracies: United States, Germany, European Union.

key_findings: Acts of attribution, non-attribution, and diffused attribution vary according to political contexts and risks; uncertainty fuels decision-making complexity; attribution serves as a strategic form of deterrence but is constrained by domestic political considerations.
main_limitations: Focus limited to liberal democracies producing possible limits on generalizability to authoritarian regimes; case selection centered on high-profile disinformation events rather than broader phenomena.
ir_scholars_relevance: Advances deterrence theory by incorporating political dimensions of attribution in the digital information environment; emphasizes the mediation of deterrence strategies by domestic political contexts in liberal democracies.

title: Pakistan's Multidirectional Balancing: A Realist Analysis of Strategic Autonomy in an Era of Great Power Competition
abstract: Pakistan's foreign policy is at its most critical crossroads as the international system is changing to multipolarity instead of American unipolarity, forcing the middle powers to find a novel approach to great power rivalry without losing their strategic autonomy. This paper discusses Pakistan's current foreign policy in terms of realism theory and explains how Pakistan has embraced the concept of a multidirectional balancing approach to the changing international system. The research illustrates that the foreign policy of Pakistan has been radically changed as a result of the Cold War-specific exclusive relationship between Pakistan and the United States to an advanced approach of contemporaneous relations with various great powers such as China, the United States, Russia, the Gulf states, and Turkey. The study uses realist theory of international relations, namely, classical realism, neorealism, defensive and offensive realism, and small state realism to interpret the behaviour of Pakistan as a state. The discussion follows the historical development of Pakistan's foreign policy since the days of Cold War alliances and post-9/11 turmoil of partnerships up to the present day, as well as multi-polar interactions that defined the strategic realignment of Pakistan. The China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) comes out as the backbone of this plan, bringing in economic capacity and a strategic layer to the future of Pakistan, which can allow it to engage in more balanced relationships with various partners, and also rebrand Pakistan as a strategic link in the connectivity networks in the region. The paper analyses the various aspects of the balancing policy of Pakistan in a methodical manner that encompasses the great power relationship, diversification in strategy towards Russia and the regional powers, regional relationship with India and Afghanistan, Middle Eastern diplomacy and involvement with the multilateral system. Nonetheless, there are major obstacles to this strategy: recurrent economic weakness that results in continued external reliance, escalating U.S.-China competition, causing the necessity to unite exclusively, instability within the region, internal political polarisation, lack of credibility among key powers, and the non-traditional form of security, especially climate change. The article has a theoretical contribution by showing how multidirectional balancing is a different approach in contrast to classical balancing, bandwagoning, or hedging, which involves simultaneous action through engagement between two or more powers. In practice, the study offers policy-relevant information on the matter of economic reform as the basis of strategic autonomy and incorporating non-traditional security threats in the planning of foreign policies. Its implications include better comprehension of the middle power behaviour within the multi-polar systems and empirically based analysis of the geopolitical South Asia in the age of the great power rivalry.

1. Introduction
Pakistan's foreign policy has traditionally been marked by strategic alignments that have been
influenced by existential security, geopolitical needs, and economic reliance. Since 1947,
Pakistan has manoeuvred through an intricate international system of regional rivalry with India,
the Cold War and territorial integrity and national survival. Throughout its history, Pakistan has
been practising a strategy of bandwagoning, where it has been allied closely to a dominant power,
the United States during the Cold War and to a more recent partnership with China to counter a
perceived threat and ensure economic and military assistance (Ch et al., 2025). But the twenty-
first century is the time that Pakistan has seen a radical change in the calculus of its strategy.
American unipolarity is being eroded, China has become a global superpower, Russia has risen,
and power is now distributed between several centres; these factors have resulted in a more fluid
and multipolar international system (Afzal & Mushtaq, 2024). At the same time, Pakistan has
undergone an enormous transformation in its internal political environment, economic issues
such as the regular balance-of-payments crisis, and changing security threats such as terrorism or
climate change, which require a re-setting of the foreign policy strategy (Ismayilov, 2020).
The modern stage of the Pakistani foreign policy is characterised by multidirectional balancing, a
policy according to which Pakistan tries to develop and preserve positive relations with several
major powers at the same time instead of being tied to one of them (Hussain et al., 2023). This
strategy was especially clear after the announcement of the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor in
2015, which strengthened Sino-Pakistani relations, but at the same time, Pakistan continued its
pragmatic relations with Iran and Central Asian states, maintaining its functional relations with
the United States, and continued to develop defence-related and energy partnerships with Russia
(Korolev, 2020). This multipolar contact is the opposite of the traditional foreign policy trends in
Pakistan and can be viewed as an active attempt to gain maximum strategic independence,
decentralisation of alliances, and escape the risks of excessive dependence on one external force
(Hussain & Ahmed).

365
Pakistan is a critical state at the crossroads of South and Central Asia, the Middle East, and
China and a pivotal point in the connectivity and security structures in the region (Shah & Khan,
2023). Since Pakistan is a nuclear-armed state with more than 240 million citizens, the stability
and strategic direction of Pakistan are of significant importance in the international peace and
prosperity, as this country is connected to some of the fundamental issues of the world, such as
nuclear proliferation, terrorism, climate change and economic development (Ziring, 2019). The
growing rivalry between the United States and China puts the nations such as Pakistan in more
challenging situations, with the growing collaboration of the country with China in the CPEC
and military cooperation, along with the historical ties to the United States, being the examples
of states caught in the crossfire between the two great powers (Ali, 2020; Khan, 2022).
Multidirectional balancing is not similar to the classic concepts of international relations: in
contrast to pure balancing, it does not create explicit alliances against certain threats; in contrast
to bandwagoning, it does not commit to a side; in contrast to hedging, it engages in active
positive interactions with multiple actors at the same time instead of being ambiguous (Ali et al.,
2022). The approach seems especially applicable to the middle powers of a multipolar system,
where structural restrictions restrict the opportunity to guarantee security on their own, but
systemic fluidity provides diplomatic possibilities (Hussain et al., 2021). The plan presupposes
the idea that in the multipolar world, single-handed alignments are associated with both great
opportunities and costs and vulnerabilities, whereas diversified engagement increases the
bargaining power, reduces dependencies and gives more strategic flexibility (Dar & Ahmad,
2024).
In this paper, the current foreign policy of Pakistan was analysed based on the realism theoretical
approach and evaluated how and why Pakistan has chosen to pursue a multidirectional balancing
strategy, as a reaction to the changing global order, and how effective and sustainable this
approach is to the security, independence, and regional stability of Pakistan (Abbas et al., 2020).
This analysis creates a theoretical framework of realism, analyzes the development of Pakistani
foreign policy throughout the Cold War alliances up to its current multidirectionalism, critically
evaluates all the dimensions of the balancing between the great power relations and the regional
dynamics and Pakistan, and determines the challenges such as economic vulnerability, the
pressures of the great power rivalry, the unstable situation in the region, and domestic political
influences. These aims serve theoretical discussions on the theme of middle power conduct in the
multipolar system and empirically based analysis on the geopolitics of South Asia in the age of
paradigm shift in international change.
2. Theoretical Framework: Realism and Multidirectional Balancing
2.1 Classical Realism: Power, Survival, and National Interest
Classical realism, which is based on the writings of Thucydides, Machiavelli and codified by
Hans Morgenthau, assumes that international politics is all about power struggles fuelled by
human nature and lack of a supreme power over states (Seton-Watson, 2019). Simply put,
classical realism believes that states are rational actors who seek national interest in terms of
power, and survival is their ultimate goal (Burbank & Cooper, 2021). The anarchic international
system is characterised by power, be it military, economic, or diplomatic, as a means and an end
of statecraft, because there is no security that can be assumed in this international system.
In the case of Pakistan, classical realist lessons are still of great importance. After gaining
independence, the foreign policy of Pakistan was widely guided by security concerns based on
its rivalry with India, territorial conflicts over Kashmir, and fears of survival in the hostile
neighbourhood (Sattar, 2023). The classical realist focus on political power politics can be used
366
to understand the reasons behind why Pakistan has consistently pursued military capacity, such
as its nuclear weapons program, and why it has been pursuing powerful external patrons to
counter material power imbalances with India (Z. A. Khan et al., 2024). Pakistan has been
making alignment decisions based on national interests, which are defined mostly in the security
framework, which led to the joining of the Cold War blocs and the development of modern
relationships with China and other prominent powers (Wu, 2018).
2.2 Neorealism and the Balance of Power System
Kenneth Waltz's neorealism or structural realism, however, changes the analytical emphasis of
human nature to the structure of the international system itself as the main determinant of state
behaviour (Sørensen et al., 2022). According to neorealism, the anarchic nature of international
politics, i.e. the lack of world government, makes states focus on survival and security by means
of self-help, which in the first place is the development of internal capabilities or the formation
of alliances with other states (Xuetong, 2019).
The neorealist notion of balance of power is especially educational in the study of Pakistan's
strategic behaviour. During the Cold War, Pakistan joined the United States in a bipolar system
that was meant to counter the influence of the Soviet Union and the non-aligned and Soviet
leaning attitude of India (Mingst et al., 2018). Yet, the unipolarity after the Cold War and the
multipolarity changes have fundamentally changed Pakistan's balancing calculus. With U.S.-
China competition creating a multipolar system, Pakistan has even more complicated options: it
cannot just be aligned with one pole and lose the other poles, nor can it be completely non-
aligned with the lack of security and economic exposure (Lundborg, 2019). The modern
multipolar order allows and even promotes the form of multidirectional balancing that would
have been challenging or impossible to achieve in a bipolar or unipolar setup (Can, 2024).
2.3 Defensive vs. Offensive Realism: Strategic Implications
There is a significant discussion in the neorealist school on defensive and offensive realism on
the extent to which states seek security and on the manner in which they seek it. According to
defensive realism, moderate balancing efforts allow states to gain security, but they must have
enough power to guarantee that they will not be killed without causing unnecessary disturbance
to others (Tabak, 2025). Offensive realism argues that states will pursue as much power and
hegemony as they can get since the anarchic system generates the irresolvable uncertainty
concerning the intentions of other states (Üstündağ, 2020).
Pakistan's actions have aspects of defensive and offensive realist logic. Its acquisition of nuclear
arms and traditional military forces can be seen as defensive realist interests of survival against
the larger opponent (Heydarian Pashakhanlou, 2018). Nonetheless, the historical emphasis on
militant proxies in Kashmir and Afghanistan, as well as the attempts to avoid the dominance of
the Indian region, used by Pakistan, are closer to the offensive realist approaches of maximising
power. The concept of multidirectional balancing can be explained as the defensive realist
approach to seeking security via diversified alliances instead of exclusive alliances that can lead
to counter-balancing (El Chaarani et al., 2022).
2.4 Small State Realism and Strategic Autonomy
The traditional realist theory mostly deals with the behaviour of great powers, but the majority of
the international actors are small and middle powers that have different strategic needs (Maass,
2020). Small state realism applies realist ideas to the unique context of states with minimal
material capabilities, focusing on survival based on smart diplomacy, alliances and taking
advantage of great power politics (Jović, 2022).
367
In the case of such states as Pakistan, strategic autonomy, or the ability to make independent
foreign policy choices without excessive external pressure, is a vital but tricky objective. Small
state realism postulates that independence is not gained in isolation but through shrewd control
of the relations with various strong actors so that no one power can play a decisive role (Aydın-
Düzgit et al., 2025; Varga) This reasoning forms the basis of the multidirectional balancing of
Pakistan: balancing between relations with the United States, China, Russia, Gulf states, and
others simultaneously, Pakistan aims to retain the freedom of decision-making and not to become
a client state of one of the patrons (Wilkins, 2018). Nonetheless, the lack of resources, territorial
weaknesses, domestic instabilities and financial reliance restrain Pakistan in its capacity to
balance between great powers or follow completely independent policies (Acharya & Buzan,
2019).
2.5 Hedging, Balancing, and Bandwagoning: Conceptual Distinctions
To get a modern approach to Pakistan, one must have an accurate conceptual definition of
various alignment strategies. According to the traditional realist theory, two major reactions to
power distributions were discovered: balancing (aligning against threats) and bandwagoning
(aligning with threatening powers) (Wang & Tan, 2021). Nevertheless, the literature after the
Cold War has identified more sophisticated approaches, specifically, the so-called hedging that
implies keeping cooperative and competitive aspects of relations with major powers open at the
same time (Spektor & Fasolin, 2018).
Hedging is described as possessing ambiguity and non-commitment, calculated diversification of
relationships to reduce risks, and maximum flexibility. Pakistan's strategy has the features of
hedging, but it proceeds to active multidirectional balancing. Instead of keeping its distance
ambiguously, Pakistan has strategically pledged to China with CPEC and defence-related
engagement, and at the same time developed relations with other rival forces (Babbar et al.,
2023). This is not non-commitment but, instead, a variety of commitments, which are handled
with caution to prevent contradiction.
2.6 Applying Realist Theory to Pakistan's Foreign Policy Behaviour
The realist theory offers a sound framework for understanding Pakistan's foreign policy based on
a number of propositions that are related to each other. To begin with, the actions of Pakistan are
inherently motivated by the factors of security in an anarchic regional and global system, and the
survival over the Indian military dominance remains to be the most important issue (Rajagopalan,
2022). Second, Pakistan logically aims to gain power, military, economic, and diplomatic, and
nuclear weapons are the final assurance of sovereignty. Third, the balance of power and disparity
in threats within its environment are calculated in choices related to alignment in Pakistan.
Fourth, the multidirectional balancing of Pakistan as a way to gain strategic autonomy is a
logical reaction to multipolarity, aimed at eliminating the weaknesses of monopolar dependence
and achieving the greatest bargaining power (Afzal & Mushtaq, 2024). Nevertheless, the
explanatory capacity of realism is not absolute; ideological forces such as Islamic identity,
domestic politics, and civil-military relationships influence the foreign policy in a manner that
cannot be explained by purely systemic realist theories (Khan, 2015).
368

3. Historical Evolution of Pakistan's Strategic Orientation
3.1 Cold War Alliances: SEATO, CENTO, and U.S. Alignment
369
The Cold War bipolarity and security rivalry between Pakistan and India were decisive in
shaping the foreign policy in the formative decades of the country. Right after gaining
independence in 1947, Pakistan faced existential problems: it had to deal with territorial conflicts
with India regarding Kashmir, there was a lack of economic resources, and the country was
militarily weaker than its giant neighbour (Hussain, 2016). These weaknesses led the leadership
of Pakistan to seek foreign security assurances from a great power patron who could offset
Indian power.
The decision-making process, based on strategic calculations, resulted in the alignment of
Pakistan with the United States and the incorporation of its strategic alignment into the structures
of the Western Cold War alliances. Pakistan became a member of the Southeast Asia Treaty
Organisation (SEATO) in 1954 and was a member of the Central Treaty Organisation (CENTO)
in 1955 (Ali & Anwar, 2023). The U.S.-Pakistan relationship turned into the staple of the foreign
policy of Pakistan, where Islamabad provided the strategic access and intelligence cooperation
and Washington, weapons, economic aid, and security guarantees (Brands & Gaddis, 2021).
Nevertheless, this correlation was not that fruitful, as the anticipations of the Americans to
support Pakistan in its fight against India were constantly undermined, and, most prominently,
during the 1965 Indo-Pakistani war, when the US imposed an arms embargo on the country (Gul
et al., 2025).
3.2 Strategic Realignments: 1971 War and the Soviet-Afghan Conflict
Two significant events occurred in the 1970s and 1980s that completely changed Pakistan's

al., 2025). The United States did not offer much in terms of assistance in the conflict, which

Unit of analysis: The foreign policy behavior of Pakistan as a middle power within the international system.

Time period studied: From Pakistan's independence in 1947 through the Cold War, post-9/11 era, up to the present day multipolar system emerging after 2015.

Geographic focus: South Asia and broader Eurasian region, including China, United States, Russia, Gulf states, Central Asia, and Afghanistan.

Identification strategy: Analytical application of realist theory variants to interpret Pakistan’s behavior via historical foreign policy shifts and strategic decisions, particularly multidirectional balancing as a response to the transition from unipolarity to multipolarity.

Key findings: Pakistan has shifted from exclusive alignments (with the US during the Cold War) to engaging multiple great powers simultaneously, using economic projects like CPEC as strategic leverage; multidirectional balancing enhances Pakistan's bargaining power and strategic flexibility but is constrained by economic weakness, regional instability, and great power pressures.

Main limitations: The analysis relies on secondary qualitative data without empirical causal testing, and realism alone cannot fully explain ideational factors like domestic politics and identity influencing foreign policy.

Why this matters for IR scholars: The paper contributes to understanding middle power behavior and strategic autonomy in multipolarity, enriching realist theory with concepts of multidirectional balancing and offering empirical insights into South Asian geopolitics amid great power rivalry.

Why this matters for strategic infrastructure research: Highlights the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) as a strategic infrastructure project central to Pakistan’s foreign policy and multipolar engagement, demonstrating how such infrastructure underpins geopolitical strategy, economic capacity, and strategic autonomy in great power competition.

title: The crisis of the conservative international order
abstract: Abstract The crisis of the liberal international order (LIO) is the dominant narrative of our time. It pervades scholarship, journalism and policy discussion, influencing the ways we see contemporary global tensions, future possibilities and political choices. This article argues that the current crisis is not simply a crisis of the LIO, but of the CIO—the conservative international order. The postwar order was not constructed by liberals alone. It was also built by conservative governments, politicians and intellectuals who were crucial parts of the domestic and international accommodations and alliances underpinning the postwar order. Today's crisis is to a large degree the result of the implosion that has transformed conservatism from a supporter of the LIO to one of its most powerful opponents. While this article focuses on the United States, the implications of the crisis of the CIO extend beyond America and require a fundamental rethinking of the conventional International Relations view of liberalism and the development of the LIO. The influence of the anti-liberal forces in American conservatism is supported by their transnational connections, allowing for powerful alliances that undermine mainstream conservatism and its historical support for the LIO. The crisis of the CIO, in short, is global.
main_argument: The current global crisis reflects not just a failure of the liberal international order but fundamentally a crisis of the conservative international order (CIO), as conservatism has shifted from supporting to opposing the postwar order.
research_design: Single-country focused analytical study with broader international implications.
dataset_or_evidence: Qualitative analysis of political discourse, historical alignment of conservative actors, and transnational conservative networks.
unit_of_analysis: Conservative international order and conservative political actors, primarily in the United States but with global transnational links.
time_period_studied: Post-World War II period to the present day (2020s).
geographic_focus: Primarily the United States with attention to global transnational conservative alliances.
identification_strategy: Tracing ideological and political shifts within conservative movements and their impact on the international order through conceptual argumentation.
key_findings: The conservative international order, historically integral to the postwar system, is now imploding as conservatism opposes the liberal international order, facilitated by transnational anti-liberal alliances that weaken mainstream conservatism’s traditional support for the LIO.
main_limitations: Lacks empirical testing through quantitative data; relies on conceptual and discursive evidence mostly focused on U.S. conservatism, which may limit generalizability.
ir_scholars_relevance: Challenges dominant IR paradigms centered on liberalism by highlighting the critical role of conservative actors in shaping the postwar order and current systemic transformations, urging a rethinking of order dynamics.

title: Damned If They Do, Damned If They Don't: The Assurance Dilemma in International Coercion
abstract: Abstract Why do some coercive demands succeed but others fail? A dominant paradigm explains coercive outcomes by pointing to the credibility and severity of threats. The concept of coercive assurance is an understudied type of commitment problem in the coercion literature. It suggests that a coercer must assure its target that its threats are conditional on the target's behavior. Many scholars overlook coercive assurance, in part because they assume it is automatic. But assurance is a crucial component of any coercive process. Even highly credible and severe threats can fail when the coercer's assurance is not credible. A novel theory, the assurance dilemma, helps to answer the following questions: Why do targets of coercion fear unconditional pain? Why do coercers punish after receiving compliance? What is the relationship between threats and assurances in coercion? The actions that a coercer can take to bolster the credibility of a threat undermine the credibility of its assurance that it will not punish the target. Targets fear that punishment may be unavoidable and thus look for assuring signals before ceding to the coercer's demands. The case of coercive bargaining over the Iranian nuclear program demonstrates the logic and effectiveness of the use of assurance.
main_argument: Coercive success depends not only on credible and severe threats but also on credible assurances that punishment is conditional, forming an assurance dilemma where efforts to strengthen threats undermine assurance credibility.
research_design: Single in-depth case study focusing on coercive bargaining over the Iranian nuclear program to illustrate the assurance dilemma.
dataset_or_evidence: Qualitative analysis of diplomatic interactions and coercive strategies during negotiations with Iran over its nuclear program.
unit_of_analysis: Coercive interactions between states, specifically the coercer-target dyad in the Iranian nuclear negotiation context.
time_period_studied: Primarily events surrounding Iranian nuclear negotiations in the early 2000s to 2020s.
geographic_focus: Iran and international actors involved in coercive diplomacy, primarily Western states and Iran.
identification_strategy: Within-case analysis demonstrating how coercers' signaling attempts exacerbate assurance dilemmas, supported by process tracing of bargaining episodes.
key_findings: Coercers’ attempts to strengthen threat credibility paradoxically weaken assurance credibility, causing targets to fear unavoidable punishment and demanding clearer assurances before compliance; this explains failures in coercive diplomacy despite credible threats.
main_limitations: Focus on a single case limits generalizability; reliance on qualitative interpretation may be subject to alternative readings; does not quantitatively measure assurance signaling effects across multiple cases.
ir_scholars_relevance: Reframes deterrence and coercion theory by highlighting assurance as a critical but understudied dimension, deepening understanding of commitment problems in coercive diplomacy.

title: The Chinese road to decarbonisation: China’s party-state capitalism in the political economy of fossil energy phase-out
abstract: While blind spots around climate change and China in the literature are now being plugged, there remains an imbalance between emphases placed on green energy build-out versus fossil energy phase-out in the political economy of global energy transition. China’s paradoxical energy economy raises the puzzle as to whether the structures of China’s party-state capitalism render it capable of successfully confronting the fossil fuel industry, just as it has scaled green technologies. This article historicises China’s fossil economy, identifying a unique potentiality for fossil energy phase-out arising from its idiosyncratic post-revolutionary development trajectory. The prominence of the CCP in China’s party-state capitalism contrasts with the West’s basis in profit-seeking market forces. This divergence underpins distinct power resources to dominate carbon-intensive industries and ideational resources to legitimate the social upheavals of energy transition. In practice, fossil energy phase-out is far from pre-determined as the potentiality rests in an ongoing struggle between corporate and political objectives within the regime as well as the uncertain responses of domestic populations and international actors. Regardless, scholars and practitioners alike should now understand China as standing alone in the world system as a geopolitically ascendent, continent-sized, post-revolutionary party-state with unique capacities to lead global energy transition.
main_argument: China’s party-state capitalism creates unique power and ideational resources that potentially enable fossil energy phase-out, differing fundamentally from Western market-driven models, but outcomes remain contingent on internal regime struggles and external responses.
research_design: Historical and political economy analysis contextualizing China’s fossil fuel trajectory within its party-state capitalism framework.
dataset_or_evidence: Qualitative historical data on China’s fossil fuel industry, party-state structures, and political economy of energy transition.
unit_of_analysis: China’s fossil energy economy and party-state capitalist regime
time_period_studied: Post-revolutionary period to present, with emphasis on contemporary transitions
geographic_focus: China
identification_strategy: Tracing historical developments and political-economic institutional continuities to explain China’s distinct potential for fossil energy phase-out.
key_findings: China’s party-state capitalism centralizes control over carbon-intensive industries and legitimizes energy transition socially and politically, creating a unique but contested potential for fossil fuel phase-out distinct from Western capitalist frameworks.
main_limitations: Focus on qualitative and historical analysis limits empirical generalizability; lacks quantitative assessment of transition success and international reaction dynamics.
ir_scholars_relevance: Reveals how China’s hybrid political-economic system challenges prevailing IR assumptions about state capacity, regime type, and global energy governance in the era of decarbonization.
strategic_infrastructure_relevance: Highlights China’s unique capacity to shape global fossil energy phase-out, informing strategic infrastructure debates around energy security, industrial policy, and geopolitical competition in great power transitions.

title: ‘We are soldiers now’: green militarism and (foreign-assisted) military training in conservation
abstract: Abstract Militarized conservation is accelerated when insecurity—violent conflict or heavily armed poaching—poses an immediate threat to wildlife and the integrity of protected areas. However, militarization often remains long after acute threats fade. To understand how violent conservation becomes an ingrained state of affairs, this article focuses on the broader geopolitics of green militarism. It explains why rangers continue to be trained for war even without any immediate security threats. Focusing on the case of Uganda, we show how the NRA/M government has extended military logics into nearly all civilian sectors and issues, including conservation. We explore how training curriculums and practices encourage park rangers in Uganda to become ‘like soldiers’ and adopt a warfare mentality. In-depth fieldwork in the Murchison Falls National Park reveals how such training represents occupational violence against the rangers themselves and contributes to their use of lethal violence against park intruders. This training is provided both by the Ugandan army and through partnerships with foreign militaries and private military companies, who use the same curriculum when training soldiers for warfare. Therefore, we argue that militarization is not only prompted by immediate security threats, but by the broader geopolitics of green militarism—reflecting the political interests of authoritarian–military governments and their international backers.

The existing literature underscores how the militarization of conservation is accel-
erated when insecurity, in the form of violent conflict or heavily armed poaching 
syndicates, poses an immediate threat to wildlife and the integrity of protected 
areas.1 Yet conservation practices often remain militarized, even after such security 
threats become less acute. In this article, we argue that broader processes of green 
militarism can explain how conservation as ‘a state of war’ becomes normalized 
in certain contexts and why park rangers continue to be trained for war, even 
when there are no immediate national security threats. Such militarism serves the 
interests of the state; it extends military influence, practices and logics over many 
aspects of social and civilian life, 2 including conservation. Moreover, militarism 
is often firmly embedded in geopolitical relations. 3 For instance, foreign armies 
(including those of the United States and the United Kingdom) are increasingly 
involved in training park rangers in different African contexts. However, little 
is known about the exact curriculum (para)military park rangers receive, how 
rangers are prepared for war and how conservation as war becomes normalized.
The article focuses on the instruction notes rangers receive during trainings, 
exercises and patrol practices in Uganda’s largest protected area, the Murchison 
Falls National Park (MFNP). In the 1980s and 1990s the park was an expansive 
protected area in decay due to political instability. However, it has prospered in 
recent years as one of Uganda’s prime conservation and tourism ‘successes’. The 
Ugandan government first took a military interest in protected areas (PAs) to 
counter potential insurgency threats. Over time, conservation transformed into 
yet another National Resistance Army/Movement (NRA/M) government tool,

This article is based on 251 official interviews that one of the authors under -

W e describe how rangers are conditioned to ‘prepare for war’ against the 
‘enemy’ and how they become soldiers in the process. Furthermore, as Mushonga 
notes, the military training rangers undergo is, at times, a form of occupational 
violence against the rangers themselves. 15 As we illustrate, the extremely harsh 
everyday conditions of military training also help explain why lethal force is 
used during patrols, despite it souring park–community relations. Grounded in 
a normative commitment to non-violent conservation, this article underscores 
the importance of understanding the political and organizational contexts that 
contribute to the lethal use of force against park intruders. 16 W e advocate for a 
focus on green militarism—beyond just militarization—since conservation spaces 
broadly mirror military ideas and structures in the rest of politics and society, both 
nationally and internationally.
The next section briefly reviews the existing literature on green militarization 
and the role of (foreign-assisted) military ranger training. W e then describe three 
distinct ways in which militarism has become entrenched in Ugandan conservation 
spaces: 1) an official collaboration between the UPDF and UW A; 2) the increasing 
use of a military curriculum in ranger training; 3) lethal violence directed at park 
intruders and neighbouring communities. This extension of military control and 
logics in conservation mirrors the broader military and authoritarian tendencies

Green militarization and the ‘war for conservation’
Militarized conservation is rooted in the colonial period 17 but has intensified over 
several periods, including during a surge in elephant and rhino poaching in the 
1980s. 18 Conservation is now increasingly seen as a form of ‘low-intensity war’ and 
a cornerstone of national security. This has been most clear in the case of South 
Africa 19 but also in Kenya. 20 In some cases, poachers are framed as ‘foreigners’ 
violating countries’ territorial boundaries. In these contexts, anti-poaching opera-
tions blur the boundaries of national security 21 to create a larger security narrative 
about anti-poaching as ‘part of a broad response to both external and internal 
threats to the state’. 22 This results in what Lunstrum describes as green militariza-
tion, ‘the use of military and paramilitary personnel, training, technologies, and 
partnerships in the pursuit of conservation efforts’. 23 The securitization of conser -
vation was further propelled through various narratives that linked poaching to 
the financing of rebel groups or jihadist terrorism (for example, Al-Shabaab is 
allegedly funded with ‘white gold’—the proceeds of illegal trade in ivory—but 
such claims are not well substantiated). 24 As Neumann has argued, war became 
‘a common model and metaphor for conceptualizing and planning biodiversity 
protection in Africa’. 25
Moreover, actual war and protracted violent conflict also heightened the milita-
rization of conservation. In Botswana, for example, conflicts in nearby countries 
in the 1980s necessitated the involvement of the Botswana Defence Force (BDF) 
in conservation to deal with potential external threats: ‘though Botswana was 
not a cobelligerent, armed groups from neighboring states regularly violated its 
borders’. 26 Thus, the BDF’s involvement in parks was initially to deter intrusion 
by armed groups, not for the purposes of anti-poaching operations. 27 This was 
also the case in Uganda in the mid-1990s, when the security situation encouraged 
army deployment, especially in parks close to the border with the Democratic 
Republic of the Congo (DRC). 28 In the Virunga National Park in eastern DRC,

Main argument: Green militarism normalizes conservation as ‘a state of war,’ embedding military logics and foreign-assisted paramilitary training in conservation practices even without immediate security threats, serving both state interests and broader geopolitical agendas.

Research design: Qualitative field research combining extensive interviews, participant observation, and document analysis to analyze military training content and its sociopolitical effects in Ugandan conservation.

Method: Case Study

Dataset or evidence: 251 official interviews with rangers, UWA officials, local communities, local authorities, participant observation of ranger patrols, ranger instruction notes, and secondary literature.

Unit of analysis: Park rangers and conservation practices in Uganda’s protected areas, specifically Murchison Falls National Park.

Time period studied: 2019–2023 (fieldwork and interviews); historical context from 1980s to present.

Geographic focus: Uganda, primarily Murchison Falls National Park, with comparative insights from other African conservation sites.

Identification strategy: Triangulation of interviews, field observations, and documentary analysis to reveal how military training content and green militarism shape ranger behavior and conservation governance.

Key findings: Military ideology and foreign-assisted training condition rangers to adopt combatant roles despite reduced direct security threats, fostering lethal violence towards intruders and communities and embedding conservation within authoritarian military state practices; green militarism is also a geopolitical tool to extend foreign influence over security and conservation.

Main limitations: Focus on one country limits generalizability; reliance on qualitative data may miss broader quantitative trends; possible bias in interviewee self-reporting and access constraints to classified training materials.

Why this matters for IR scholars: Highlights the intersection of militarism, authoritarian state practices, and conservation governance, illustrating how security and environmental domains are entwined in geopolitics and state capacity debates.

Why this matters for strategic infrastructure research: Demonstrates how foreign military actors shape territorial security through environmental governance, linking conservation to wider geopolitical struggles and governance of contested spaces.

title: Political risk and firm exit: evidence from the US–China Trade War
abstract: When do political risks lead to divestment from a profitable market? Existing theories argue both that foreign investors may be sensitive to political tensions, but that they may only be sensitive to violent conflict. Using the crucial case of the US–China Trade War, we outline how political risks increased rates of exit among foreign firms while firm entrenchment mitigated these risks. Using a new dataset on all foreign-invested enterprises registered in China between 2017 and 2019, we implement triple interaction models to isolate the impact of increased political risks, investor national origin, and entrenchment on firm exit. Our findings show that heightened political risks during the trade war did increase firm exits by 34% – 3% points over the pre-conflict baseline. Tariffs, the targeted effect of the trade war, increase US firm exits by 1% point. Firm exit is determined by the balance of heightened political risks against the availability of firm-level resources to mitigate these risks. These findings reconcile the conflicting expectations of the ‘business as usual’ and ‘follow the flag’ literatures about how firms respond to political risk, highlighting the tremendous collateral damage tariffs can cause in an age of global value chains.

ABSTRACT
When do political risks lead to divestment from a profitable market? Existing theories 
argue both that foreign investors may be sensitive to political tensions, but that they 
may only be sensitive to violent conflict. Using the crucial case of the US–China 
Trade War, we outline how political risks increased rates of exit among foreign firms 
while firm entrenchment mitigated these risks. Using a new dataset on all 
foreign-invested enterprises registered in China between 2017 and 2019, we imple -
ment triple interaction models to isolate the impact of increased political risks, inves -
tor national origin, and entrenchment on firm exit. Our findings show that heightened 
political risks during the trade war did increase firm exits by 34% – 3% points – over 
the pre-conflict baseline. Tariffs, the targeted effect of the trade war, increase US firm 
exits by 1% point. Firm exit is determined by the balance of heightened political risks 
against the availability of firm-level resources to mitigate these risks. These findings 
reconcile the conflicting expectations of the ‘business as usual’ and ‘follow the flag’ 
literatures about how firms respond to political risk, highlighting the tremendous col -
lateral damage tariffs can cause in an age of global value chains.

Introduction

political risks are low (Barry, 2018; Pandya, 2016; Jensen et  al., 2012; Jensen, 2008),

DeRouen Jr., 2007; Rodman, 2001), and when property rights are protected (Wellhausen, 
2014; Biglaiser & Staats, 2012; Li et  al., 2003) . Comparatively little is known, however,

about the determinants of FDI flight, or the politics of divestment. Do elevated polit -
ical risks increase the likelihood that foreign investors exit from a once-promising 
market? When political relations sour between sender and host countries, will FDI 
‘follow the flag’ out of the market? If so, are some firms more likely to exit than others?
We build on work by Vekasi ( 2019), Barry ( 2018), Graham et  al. ( 2016) and 
Camacho and Rodriguez ( 2013) to unpack the effects of political risk on divestment. 
Previous research on the impacts of political risks and FDI flight focuses on risks 
associated with violent conflicts, such as civil wars, insurgency and terrorism, demon -
strating how MNCs’ behavior depends on the different stages of the FDI lifecycle. 
While the probability of FDI entry decreases with conflict duration and intensity, 
once the costs of investment are sunk, firms are resilient to all but the most intense 
forms of political risks, and FDI exits are rare (Barry, 2018). Firms with the same 
national origins act similarly because of a sense of ‘shared political risk’ (Wellhausen, 
2014). We expand the literature on FDI exit by examining how MNCs respond to an 
important episode of non-violent political risk: The US–China Trade War.
Even before the trade war, China represented a crucial case for understanding 
both FDI investment and divestment. China is one of only two non-US allies 
among the top 20 largest recipients of FDI stocks between 2005 and 2022, 1 making 
China a crucial case for understanding variation in firm exits as both a geopolitical 
rival to the US and the second largest recipient of FDI in the world, trailing behind 
only the US. The US–China Trade War offers a unique opportunity to examine the 
impact of political risk outside of armed conflicts. The trade war represents the 
most serious disruption to global supply chains since their emergence. Studying the 
effects of political risks on FDI in this influential case could help establish the 
scope conditions for a theory of FDI outflows. On the one hand, we would expect 
national origin of the firm to be the most salient in this case where geopolitics 
looms so large. On the other hand, the size and depth of the Chinese market may 
convince some foreign investors to ignore pressures from their home governments 
to decouple from China.
We argue that the 2018 US–China Trade War increased political risks across the 
board for all foreign MNCs operating in China, contributing to the exit of some 
China-based subsidiaries. Costs of business increase through concrete measures 
such as tariffs and export controls but political risks also increase intangible costs, 
such as uncertainty about the future business environment and political pressure 
from sender governments as well.
These factors drive political risk for China-based operations by raising costs and 
changing the rules of the game, with significant ramifications for overseas produc -
tion. But some firms resist the influence of these adverse effects of intensifying 
geopolitical competition through greater entrenchment in the local market. We uti -
lize micro-level data from the original Foreign-Invested Enterprises in China (FIEC) 
Dataset to implement triple interaction models identifying the conditions under 
which the trade war increased divestment through firm exit. We find that the blunt 
effect of the trade war – the souring of business relations felt by all MNCs oper -
ating in China – was significant, increasing MNC subsidiary exit by an average of 
3% points, or approximately a 34% increase over pre-trade war levels. We find that 
US firms in industry classes with higher tariffs – the targeted effect of the trade 
war – were marginally more likely to exit than MNCs from other countries in the 
same industries by approximately 1% point. Firms from countries with close

not exit at a higher rate when tariffed, but still suffer significant blunt effects of 
the trade war. Finally, firm entrenchment in China mitigates the effect of rising 
political risks, reducing firm exits. These results are consistent with the emerging 
literature on the heterogeneous impact of political risk on domestic economic 
actors (Vekasi, 2019; Li & Liu, 2019; Davis & Meunier, 2011; Kastner, 2007). The 
trade war increased overall firm exits but had a heterogeneous effect in terms of 
which MNCs exited China.
Our results have significant theoretical and empirical implications for under -
standing the dynamics of FDI flows, especially between geopolitical competitors. 
Theoretically, we present one of the first systematic attempts to understand divest -
ment through firm exit during a clearly demarcated period of heightened political 
risk. We show that the interaction of heightened macro risk and the differing 
capacity for firms to mitigate micro risk drives firm exits. Empirically, we provide 
evidence that the trade war elevated political risks for all foreign MNCs in China, 
but tariffs marginally accelerate FDI exits in affected industries. The trade war had 
a greater blunt effect than targeted effect, with smaller and newer firms bearing the 
brunt of its impact. This suggests policy initiatives using tariffs to encourage the 
re-shoring of specific industries may have limited effects and carry unintended dis -
tributional consequences. Our results also explain the uneasy coexistence of eco -
nomic decoupling with business-as-usual found in the current era of the US–China 
Trade War. They help explain why the anecdotal evidence on how much decou -
pling or derisking is actually happening as a result of Western politicians pressur -
ing MNCs to divest from China is mixed. Finally, our research highlights the need 
to analyze political risk outside of the extreme case of violent conflict.
The case: the US–China Trade War
After accusing China of unfair trade practices and intellectual property theft, the 
Trump administration imposed four rounds of tariffs on Chinese goods between 
July 2018 and May 2019, specifically targeting intermediate and capital goods sup -
ported by the ‘Made in China 2025 Initiative’ which quickly expanded to include 
a wide array of consumer goods as well (Zhang, 2022). Chinese officials retaliated 
with four rounds of tariffs on US goods, such as soybeans, whose production was 
concentrated in Republican-supporting districts (Kim & Margalit, 2021).
The US–China Trade War quickly expanded beyond tariffs to a wider set of 
policies aimed at the ‘strategic decoupling’ of the two economies. A slew of other 
policy measures designed to curb Chinese competitiveness in emerging technolo -
gies – the so called ‘tech-war’ – and to heighten ideological competition between 
the two systems of government – the so-called ‘new cold war’ – accompanied the 
escalation of tariffs. Since 2018, the Department of Commerce added more than 
600 Chinese companies, including Huawei, one of the world’s largest information 
and communication technology suppliers, to a list of entities subject to stringent 
export licensing requirements for US technology. The US Congress expanded con -
trols via the Export Controls Reform Act to cover dual-use emerging and founda -
tional technologies and also increased scrutiny of Chinese investment in dual-use, 
high-technology sectors via the Foreign Investment Risk Review Modernization Act 
of 2018. The Department of the Treasury expanded the Office of Foreign Asset
